ONTARIO HOURS OP WORK AND VACATIONS WITH PAY ACT

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That on Saturday, the 29th July, 1944, and every Saturday thereafter until the end of the present session, the house shall meet at 11 o'clock a.m., and the order of business and procedure shall be the same as on Fridays.
May I ask the Prime Minister how many Saturdays he has in mind?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I hope there will not be more than one.

Mr. Speaker, the members of this group are not satisfied to let the motion pass without some explanation from the Prime Minister as to how many Saturdays it is anticipated we may be here. If this motion means that we are to sit Saturdays only for the purpose of handling routine business, that we are to sit one or two Saturdays in order to get the business of the house over with, we would be quite satisfied to agree to it. However, there is a lot of important new legislation coming in at the tail end of the session. The house is now sitting morning, noon and night throughout the week, and in order to familiarize ourselves with the new legislation, in order to try to understand what is going through the house, we require at least our Saturdays to catch up with our work. Those of ns who have to remain here all the time while the house is sitting find it rather hard. The business that still has to go through the house is of extreme importance, particularly the new legislation which must be scrutinized carefully if we are to understand what it is all about and protect the Canadian people in the process of its going through.
You are not the only one who is protecting them.

You speak for yourself. I am asking the Prime Minister if it is possible for him to indicate what the length of the session will be. Otherwise we are not in favour of this motion to sit on Saturdays, morning, noon and night, in addition to working the rest of the week on the same basis. We figure that we cannot handle the work of the house as it should be handled.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I should like to be able to give my hon. friend a precise answer, but when he asks me how much time will be occupied by hon. gentlemen opposite, I have to say to him that I cannot possibly

Saturday Sittings
tell. The length of the session, onee the sessional programme is announced, depends more on the opposition than it does on the government. Unfortunately I cannot say how much time hon. gentlemen may wish to take in discussing the measures that are before the house. What I would point out to the hon. member is that there will be no legislation coming down that I am aware of at the moment to which reference was not made in the speech from the throne and the introduction of which hon. members have had knowledge of since the beginning of the session, or one or two measures since announced, the purport of which they are already aware. It is quite true that some of the bills have not been before the house, but I think hon. members have a pretty good idea of what will be contained in the bills. I point that out to make clear that the government is not trying to do anything exceptional at the present time.
There are still estimates to pass. These have been before members of parliament since the beginning of the session. There will be nothing new under that heading except the supplementary estimates that may be brought down.
It has always been necessary in the winding up of the business of a session to have morning and Saturday sittings, and I have tried as far as I could to judge what the wish of the house might be and have the wish of hon. members carried out. I think it was July 24, just a year ago to-day, that the previous session of parliament concluded. It looks as though this session, which opened almost the same time in January of this year, is going to run on some little time longer. But I do believe hon. members hope- we may wind up the business without very much in the way of delay.
My hon. friend says, "we are here all the time," but I have not seen either his leader or the leader of the Social Credit group in this house for a week or more past. After all, leaders do count for something, or ought to count for something whenever reference is made to a party as a whole. I would say to my hon. friend that the disposition of the government will be to try to arrange Saturday business in a way that will be generally acceptable. We will not seek to bring on contentious measures on Saturdays, but I think we could get th'-ough a good deal of business in the way of estimates.
I hope there will not be any exception taken to this motion because I really believe it d^0' meet with the general wish of those who desire to wind up the business of this session as soon as possible.
This shows clearly the folly of the Prime Minister's motion which washed out all sittings on Wednesdays during the body of the session, thus losing much irreplaceable time.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I would like to make a brief observation with_respect to what has passed between the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Cape Breton South. There is something in what the hon. member for Cape Breton South says with respect to the burden which those of us in opposition have to carry as well as the members of the government. This burden falls particularly upon those of us who have to be in our seats practically all the time in order to watch the legislation. It does not give us very much time to study the legislation.
Perhaps the Prime Minister would be good enough to consider this question a week from Friday. If at that time the house is not within a reasonable distance of concluding its work, perhaps we may have that Saturday off, having in mind the circumstances as they then are. I would have no objection to the motion going through on the understanding that the Prime Minister keep in mind the possibility of thus reviewing the position.
When the Prime Minister says that the length of the session is governed solely by the opposition-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not solely.

I took it from his remark that he had the opposition largely in mind so far as the extending of the length of the session was concerned. I must say to the Prime Minister that the opposition needs a certain amount of time to give proper attention to the measures that come before the house. Having that definitely in mind may I point out to the Prime Minister that this is an unusual session from the government's point of view. I do not think since I came into the house there has been a session in which there were so many bills to be dealt with in the last few moments which had not been seen at all by the members of the house. The government will have to take some responsibility in that regard, because the opposition cannot be expected at the last minute to go through all the estimates and study important bills that have not yet come before the house and conclude the session within a few days. We have to consider that our job first of all is to criticize properly these bills as they come before us, no matter how long we may have to stay here to do it; but that does not mean of course that we should waste time in useless debate and repetition.
Farm Prices

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I take no exception to my hon. friend doing everything possible to protect the full rights of the opposition, and I agree that criticism is helpful. But I do take exception to the attitude that the government is always trying to put something over. The measures which the government is bringing down are obviously in the interests of the people, and I would hope that the opposition would join with the government in seeking to place these measures on the statutes as soon as possible.
As to a week from Friday, may I say to my hon. friend that in reviewing the situation I have been asking myself very seriously whether, if this session is going to ran on very much longer, it would not be better to adjourn over August and September and meet again in October and November. I do not want to do that, because I do not think hon. members wish to do it, but that is an aspect of the situation which will have to be considered in any review that may be made. May I say to my hon. friend, with regard to what may be done a week from Saturday, that sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext: On the c.-ders of the day:

subtopic: POSSIBLE STOPPAGE OF WORK AT HALIEAX SHIPYARDS
speechtext:
On Friday last the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) asked a question with reference to the dispute in the Halifax shipyards, I replied that as I had just returned to the city I would be glad to give him a reply on Monday.
The answer is that we are doing everything possible to avert a stoppage of work in this vital industry. The senior industrial relations officer of the department in the maritime provinces is at present in Halifax conferring with union and company officials with reference to their differences of opinion with a view to bringing about agreement between them.
I have received a number of telegrams from trade unions in the Halifax district suggesting that the company be compelled to implement the report of the conciliation board. Without saying anything that might prejudice the negotiations about to commence, I would merely state that neither the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act nor the wartime labour relations regulations which superseded that act requires the acceptance of recommendations in reports of conciliation boards by the parties concerned.	Trade unions	and
employer's organizations generally are opposed to any such step. I would say this, however, that the labour relations regulations compel employers and employees to bargain collectively, but do not obligate an employer to agree to the closed shop or check-off of union dues, which is the issue in this dispute.

The leader of the opposition on Friday referred to a matter which had arisen in the other house and which he stated had to do with the privileges of parliament. May I give my hon. friend an answer as to my position in this matter by referring to an old and well-known rule:
Whatever matter arises concerning either house of (parliament ought to be discussed and adjudged in that house to which it relates land not elsewhere.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REFERENCE TO QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE (MR. GRAYDON) ON JULY 21
speechtext: May I say to the Prime Minister that it was not with respect to a debate in the other house that I was referring. It was a case of a member of parliament having made a statement in parliament and then being dismissed because he had made the statement. That, in my opinion, constitutes an interference with the freedom of speech of members of parliament, and for that reason I felt that the Prime Minister and the leader of the government in the other house should have a conference with respect to the matter because I very definitely feel that in this incident there is involved an issue of considerable magnitude.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REFERENCE TO QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE (MR. GRAYDON) ON JULY 21
speechtext: I say to my hon. friend that if he wishes to raise an issue of much larger magnitude he would ask this federal government or any member of it to begin to criticize the action of a provincial government. It has taken that responsibility and is exercising it in its full rights, and this house of parliament should be the last to seek to invade the jurisdiction of a province by criticizing the action of a government in relation to its own officials.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. This bill is to provide:
(a)	one-twelfth of all the items to be voted in the main estimates for the fiscal year 1944-45;
(b)	an additional one-sixth of the five services detailed in the schedule to the bill.
The proportion of one-twelfth for all services is intended to provide for ordinary requirements to the end of August.
The additional one-sixth for certain special votes is necessary owing to the seasonal nature of the services provided. The first three items provide for the expenses of the Senate and House of Commons which are heavier in the early part of the fiscal year. The other two items are to cover geological and topographical surveys where expenses of sending out field parties must be undertaken early in the season in order that projects may be completed within the few months suitable for this work.
Two bills each providing for one-sixth of all items to be voted in the estimates for 1944-45 have already been granted. These were to provide for requirements to July 31. There were no schedules in these previous bills as provision was made for a uniform proportion for all services.
The present bill provides for one-twelfth generally and an additional one-sixth for the special services referred to and is in exactly the same form as bills of previous years providing for similar services.

Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Judges Act to provide that a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, the Exchequer Court of Canada or of any superior court, county court or the circuit court of the district of Montreal, may elect, in lieu of a pension or annuity as presently authorized under the said act. to divide his annuity so that his wife will receive an annuity equal to one-third thereof, and that if he should die in office that his widow will receive an annuity equal to [DOT] two-ninths or one-ninth, in certain cases, of his salary.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Bradette in the chair.
Judges Act

With the general
principle of the resolution I think most hon. members are in agreement. Up to the present the situation in this country has been such that no opportunity under the law has been given to judges, many of whom have sacrificed large incomes in order to serve on the bench, to make due provision for their wives by the voluntary assignment of the allowances they would receive at the conclusion of a period of service. This whole matter brings into review the question of judicial reform and the necessity of facing this important problem at the very earliest possible day. Too often appointments to the judiciary in the past have been based on political services, and too often the qualification for appointment to the bench has been the fact that the applicant has been defeated for public office. I remember one occasion particularly when a member of the Canadian bar, referring to the system in the United States under which, with the exception of the supreme court and the federal courts the members of the judiciary are elected, said that there was very little difference between the system in Canada and that in the United States. That difference, he said, was that in the United States one had to be elected to be a judge, whereas in Canada the qualification too often was that one had been defeated two or three times.
I believe this resolution is evidence of the recognition by the Minister of Justice of the necessity of doing everything possible to ensure that the best possible men, eminent leaders of the bar, shall accept appointment to the bench. I do not believe there is one of us who was not distressed the other evening by the statement made by the minister that three outstanding members of the bar in Canada who had been offered appointments to the Supreme Court of Canada had refused because it would have meant too great a sacrifice. It is interesting to know that in the intervening seventy-five years since confederation, the salaries of the judiciary have more or less continued to fall lower and lower. The cost of living since confederation has gone up some 500 per cent, and during the same time the income of the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada and those of judges of courts of appeal, after deducting present-day taxes, are lower by $1,524 a year than at confederation.
To-day, having regard to the ramifications of business and the expansion of commerce, it is even more necessary than it was at that time to have outstanding members of the bar accept appointment to our courts. The judges of the superior courts in the provinces receive

to-day, after deduction of taxes, $934 a year less than they did seventyffive years ago. May I add that it was recommended as far back as 1929 that consideration be given to increases of judges' salaries. There is no provision today for the survivors of judges after they pass on, and this resolution is to cover that.
Some may argue that our judges are exceptionally well paid but a comparison with the amounts paid in other countries will show that we in this country are endeavouring to enlist the best possible brains to the bench while giving the least returns. In asking men to go on the bench with the low return that is available to them we are in fact encouraging the appointment of members of the bar who are not outstanding, and in not having compulsory retirement of judges at seventy-five years we are continuing to penalize litigants in that they are required to have their cases tried before superior court judges a number of whom are unfit because of age and physical disability to perform properly the duties of their office.
I mentioned a moment ago the salaries in other countries. Let me compare the salary of the chief justices of Canada with judges holding similar or comparable positions in other countries. A judge holding a comparable position in England receives a salary of $30,000 a year, with $18,750 pension after fifteen years; in Scotland, $18,000; Irish Fret State, $15,000; Northern Ireland, $20,000; Australia, from $13,000 to $15,000; New Zealand, $11,500; South Africa, $13,750 to $16,250. A comparable position in the various states of the United States pays $22,500.
I think it will be agreed that the resolution which has been introduced is a step in the right direction. It recognizes the problem of assuring the best judicial appointments in every province. It recognizes the need of giving men who accept appointment to the bench the opportunity to make provision for their dependents, and the minister is to be congratulated on this forward step. I believe that a committee should be set up

it is too late to do it this session-at the next session to look into the matter of an age limit for the judiciary. Seventy-five has -been suggested in many provinces. If the best men are to be mobilized for the bench of this country; if we are not only to assure litigants but to convince them that they will receive justice when they go to our courts, early consideration must be given to reducing the age at which judges shall be retired from the bench. Personally I believe consideration should be

Judges Act
given in many cases to retirement, or at least the opportunity given to judges to retire, at the age of seventy.
Parliament often seems to fall behind the demands of public opinion outside of the house. This resolution represents the point of view that is held outside this house by laymen on every hand. It recognizes the need for judicial reform. It recognizes that everything must be done toward maintaining the highest possible standard of justice. These things can be secured only if the law makes such provision as is necessary to secure the best possible men on the .bench.

In my judgment this is a very worth-while and commendable piece of legislation. I am in entire accord with the principle of the resolution. The details we shall necessarily have to leave until the bill has been introduced, but in so far as it is a step in the direction of making the position of the judiciary more secure I am heartily in accord with it.
I have always believed that having regard to the importance of the administration of justice, affecting as it does not only property but in many cases the life of the individual, the judiciary should be entirely free from financial worries. This is a step which has been recommended by the bar and by the judges of this country for many years. I am glad indeed to see that the Minister of Justice has taken cognizance of the stand which has been taken by these bodies. Generally speaking, I believe that the income of the judges is too low in comparison with comparable positions. I agree with the hon. member for Lake Centre when he says that in order to attract to the bench the very best type of man we shall have to put the judiciary in a better financial position than it is at the present time. There are certain provinces in which the emoluments of office are attractive, and in which there is no difficulty in obtaining appointments, but in other provinces where the practice of law is more lucrative, I believe I am right in saying that the administration has much more difficulty in obtaining the services of the very best legal men.
The Minister of Justice mentioned the other day that he had a certain amount of difficulty in obtaining appointments to the supreme court; that he had approached three men who he believed would be admirable appointments, but in each case they felt that for personal reasons they could not accept. I take it that at least one of the reasons had to do with the financial position. If we are to attract the best type of men to the bench we shall have
to review this whole matter of judicial salaries in the very near future. There is no doubt that for many years the judges have been concerned about the position in which their widows and dependents would be placed if they passed on. It must be apparent to everyone that any occasion for such concern on the part of judges should be avoided if at all possible.
May I suggest to the minister that in addition to the measure which he has introduced to-day he consider doing something for the widows of judges who have passed on? In some cases they have been left penniless. Such a state of affairs should not have been allowed to exist. The minister has now introduced legislation which will help to avoid that in the future; but I suggest that he review the situation with the object of endeavouring to deal with the matter. I know of the widow of one judge who passed on a few years ago. In all fairness she should be placed in the same position as the wife who will benefit from this legislation.
I should like to commend this piece of legislation as a worth-while and forward step in so far as the judiciary and the bar of this country are concerned, and one which I believe will receive the support of the general public.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I should like to say a few words, so as to put clearly before the committee, and so that it may be reported to the country, the purport and effect of this legislation. Hon. members who have spoken know how fully I agree with everything they have said, with the possible exception of the suggestion that it is still a requisite for recommendation to the bench, to have been defeated in some political campaign. With that I do not agree, because as a lawyer I really do take some pride in the appointments it has been my privilege to recommend since assuming office, especially appointments to the high courts. I should like to say as much about the appointments to the county courts- and possibly I would be able to do so if I knew the appointees before their appointment as well as it has been my privilege to know those I have recommended to the higher courts.
However the situation at the present time is that we are still in a war. We have ceilings-we hope;-on the purchasing power of a dollar and also ceilings on wages and salaries. I fully appreciate the position in which those who are administering justice in this country find themselves, squeezed as they are between a salary that cannot be increased and a rate of taxation that takes from them a very substantial portion of what was looked
Judges Act

upon before as being only what they required to maintain the positions to which they have been appointed. But we are all feeling the pinch. Under present conditions, although I considered and discussed all the factors mentioned by hon. members, it was felt that nothing which would put a further burden on the exchequer in a time of war could be contemplated for the judges-because if it were done for the judges, a line could not be drawn. Only a few days ago we had a long debate over the situation as it applies to members of parliament, in which we discussed the amount fixed as indemnity to members, and the rate of taxation which prevails. We know however that pressure is upon prectically everybody, with the exception of those whose remuneration for ordinary labour has been improved; above that level the pressure is on everybody.
It is 'well known to hon. members that there is now pending before the national war labour board an application respecting a class .of very worthy participants in the industrial and economic life of our country. I refer to the brotherhood of railway employees. That application is for an increase, because of the position in which they find themselves, as a result of increased taxation. Now, if that brotherhood, and the members thereof, were to receive an increase, I think it would be necessary that it spread, because the whole of the workers of Canada might well say the railway employees are no worse off than other classes of Canadian workers or Canadian persons receiving wages or salaries. And if that did happen it would be the end of such control as it has been possible to maintain against inflation. I offer that as my excuse for not bringing in this bill at an earlier stage in the session. I wanted to wait until the budget was brought down, and to see if there was anything that could be done by way of relief, even though it did impose something upon the exchequer. When the budget was brought down, and when it was determined what the budget would be, it became apparent that nothing involving any substantial expense for the country could be done for the judges at the present time. I then suggested that what was already on the statute book, in the form of pensions, be left there, for those who would wish to take the benefit of it as it exists, and that there be an option given to judges who are .low on the bench, or to those who may be appointed, to say that instead of taking the who'e pension for themselves they would prefer a pension of two-thirds and they would have an allocation of one-third of it to their wives.
[Mr St. Laurent.]
The result will be that the exchequer will not in the long run bear any more-or should not bear any more than it is at the present time.
Just as an illustration: for the ordinary high court judge the salary is S9,000. The pension to which he is entitled on retirement is two-thirds of that, or $6,000. He will have the privilege of saying, "Instead of providing me with a pension for life of $6,000, provide me with a pension for life of $4,000, and provide my wife with a pension for life of $2,000. While we both live we will get $6,000, and when one of us dies the other will continue to receive his or her portion of the pension." In the long run it will work out in a way which will not, or should not cost the treasury anything more than the present system. For those who take the option, or those who say, or who will say between now and November 1, that they are bound by an irrevocable option that they wish to reduce their rights to two-thirds of what they are, leaving the other third for the benefit of their consorts, there will be a further provision that if the judge dies in office the consort will get one-third of what the judge's pension would have been at retirement-that is to say, two-ninths of what his salary was. That applies to all cases of the supreme court, the exchequer court, the high courts-that is, superior courts-or the courts of appeal in the provinces.

If a judge died at the end of four years' service, would a pension be payable to his widow?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes. If a judge is appointed and becomes incompetent to carry on his judicial duties, even after only two years of service on the bench, he gets a pension of two-thirds of his salary. That has happened within recent years, to the knowledge of the hon. member and myself. A chief justice of Ontario, the predecessor of the present chief justice, was in office only a very short time. But when because of his health it became necessary that he retire, he got a pension of two-thirds of his emolument. That is the rule which has been on the statute book since 1920 with respect to high court judges.
There is a difference in connection with county courts or district court judges or judges of the circuit courts of Montreal. If they have not been on the bench five years, they get only one-third instead of two-thirds. It is for that reason the resolution provides that there will be some cases in which the widow would receive only one-ninth instead of two-ninths.

Judges Act
In every case we say to the judge, "We are not going to take from you anything the statute now gives you. If you wish to take an irrevocable option, however, to be satisfied with only two-thirds of what the statute gives you, we wiii give the other third to your wife." That is all But, in fact, it will create a sense of some security for a great many of those who occupy judicial positions. Formerly it may have been possible for them to protect their families by taking out insurance. But I know from my own experience that since the present rates of taxation have been in force it is not possible to pay insurance premiums. Many cannot continue to pay them.

And there is the other situation, too, that a judge may not be in sufficiently good health to get insurance.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Possibly; but that is something for which at the present time I do not think we can take responsibility. But we did appoint gentlemen to the bench who felt that they were going to be able to carry insurance for the protection of their families; and we did find ourselves forced into a situation where taxation which impairs that possibility for them had to be imposed. That being so, we say to them, "You are entitled to a pension; if you will be satisfied with two-thirds of it for yourself we will allow you to contribute the other one-third to your wife; if she outlives you, she will continue to receive it; if she predeceases you, you will have only the two-thirds; it is left to you to say." That is something about which each individual will be entitled to exercise his option. If he does not like it, he can continue with the terms of the statute as it is. On the whole I do not anticipate that there will be any real extra burden placed upon the exchequer.
The other matters are such that I hope they will receive from the Department of Justice, whoever may be there, and from this house whatever the majority may be, the most sympathetic consideration. I think it is in the interests of this country that the best possible lawyers be attracted to the bench. That was so in the past. It is only in the last quarter of a century that the economy of the nation has got into such a condition that a position on the bench ceases to be comparable with the position a successful lawyer is able to make for himself, even in the big cities.
I think the British system of recruiting judges from the practising profession is a good system. Whenever general conditions make it possible I think we will have to get back to
the situation that existed at confederation. As the hon. member for Lake Centre has pointed out, at that time the purchasing power of the dollar was five times what it is at the present time and the emoluments provided were such as to attract the most successful practitioners. I think it will be in the interests of the Canadian people to maintain the high standards of our courts of justice.
In conclusion I want to pay a tribute, which I think will be shared by all members of this house, to our judiciary. I want to comment upon the high regard in which it has been held by the Canadian people since confederation..

Has any consideration been given to the suggestion I made with respect to existing widows of judges?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That was considered but it was not felt that anything could be done at this time, especially under our system of not interfering with the freeezing orders and so forth. It would be doing something new. I think the widows of judges who have passed on will find themselves with an almost irresistible case just as soon as conditions are such that some readjustments can be made. But I would not undertake to do this at the present time because if it were done it would be said that we were doing something for one class of people. We are just allowing the judges to make provision out of what they are entitled to under the present law. It would not be the same principle if we extended it. The judge who has passed on would not have had an opportunity of exercising this option, and no one can say how he would have exercised it. That is something that I think will have to be considered on the basis of its being a new grant. I cannot take the responsibility of asking parliament to make a new grant this year, but I do take the responsibility of asking parliament to say to the judges, " You have a grant and we will allow you to rearrange it."

I agree that these widows
have an almost irresistible case, and I think it is almost irresistible at- the present time. The latter part of the resolution contains something new.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If my hon. friend will pardon me, I do not look upon it as something new. This is something only for the widows of judges who exercise their option between now and November 1 or within ninety
Judges Act

days after their appointment. They will make an option in writing reducing their own rights to two-thirds off what they would' otherwise have the right to receive and applying the other third to their consorts. I do not think that is anything entirely new.

I agree with that, but the new part is that should a judge die in office an annuity of two-ninths or one-ninth will be paid to his widow. That is not the case at the present time.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That is only with respect to the widows of judges who will have exercised their options. If a judge upon appointment prefers to keep the situation as it is, and he dies in office, his widow would not be entitled to any pension. This pension of one-third will go only to the widows of judges who will have exercised their option at the outset, saying that their pension rights are to be divided between themselves and their wives.

I quite understand that as a consideration that is required, but he is getting two benefits. First, he has the benefit of being allowed to continue one-third of his pension to his wife after he dies, provided that the pension is payable. Under this part a man may be in office only for a year. Should he die, his widow will be entitled to a pension for the rest of her life. I agree with that, but I would like to see the Widows of judges who have died within the last year- I would not confine it to a year but I take that as an example-placed in the position where they would receive a pension. After November 1 when a judge dies his widow will be in that position, provided of course that he accepts this proposition; she will receive an annuity for the rest of her life. I merely point out to the minister that I think it desirable that something be done for these widows. I understand that this one-ninth provision applies to county court and district court judges?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It applies to county court and district court judges who have not been in office five years. Under the act as it is, if a county court judge retires, having been in office for less than five years and being under seventy-five years of age, he cannot get a pension of more than one-third of his salary. If he has been in office more than five years, he gets a pension of two-thirds of his salary. One-third of two-thirds is two-ninths, and one-third of one-third is one-ninth.

After November 1 a judge appointed to the bench would have to exercise that option?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Those who are on the bench at the present time will have until November 1 of this year to exercise this irrevocable option; those who are appointed will have ninety days to do so from the date of their appointment.

Suppose a man is married after he becomes a judge; will he have the same opportunity?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Under the bill as will be submitted to the house he will have no opportunity to make any new option. Some cases may occur where it is desirable that something should be done, but I do not think there will be many. When a man is appointed he should realize his position and be able to make a decision as to how he wants his pension rights treated. If he thinks he is going to be married he can say, "I will be content with two-thirds of my pension and I will leave the other third available for the woman I am going to marry."

I take it that you do not insist upon any declaration on that point.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No.

How many judges will be affected by this? Is it 250 or thereabouts?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: There are 96 judges in Ontario, 53 in Quebec, 30 in Saskatchewan, 23 in Alberta, 25 in British Columbia, 40 in Nova Scotia, 13 in New Brunswick, and 6 in Prince Edward Island.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I feel that the terms of this resolution as outlined by the minister are sound and that it is a good piece of legislation he is bringing down. I agree too with the desire expressed with those who have spoken thus far in this debate that everything possible should be done to strengthen the position of our judiciary. It is of extreme importance that all care be taken in this matter. I support, as hon. members know, the suggestion that has been made a number of times that one of the means of strengthening the judiciary is that a compulsory retirement age be set throughout. On the question of salaries and pensions, however, I feel that there is one comment that should be made before we pass this resolution. In line with what I have just said, I am not opposed at all to improving the salary position or the

Judges Act
pension position of our judges, but it seems to me that we should maintain a .proper perspective in this matter. I observe from the estimates that there is set aside this year the sum of $311,466.64 to provide pensions for fifty-six judges now on the retired list. That is an average pension of over $5,560 for each of those judges. Considering the honour that has been theirs because of the positions which they have held, such pensions are not too bad: considering also the terribly small amount of the old age pension that we pay to others of our honoured citizens reaching the age of seventy, I feel that we should be giving prior concern to that other group of people. I support this resolution and the suggestions that have been made by hon. members, but I urge that in the matter of the old age pension, before we worry too much about those who are receiving over $5,560 a year on an average, we should be giving some real concern to those to whom we are paying only $300 a year or less.

How many widows of judges are now living in Canada?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am sorry I have not that figure. I got it some two years ago and as I remember it, it was quite a large number. I would not venture, however, to mention a figure at this moment because my memory is not sufficiently clear. I went into it at that time and even had an actuarial calculation made as to what would be the cost of pensions on various scales for the widows of deceased judges, and it was a substantial sum.

Has any estimate been made of how much it is expected will come out of the treasury under this arrangement? Based on ordinary mortality rates there may be a considerable additional sum payable out of the treasury by reason of the introduction of this measure.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It is not possible to make any calculation with respect to the first portion. It is not expected to mean any burden over a period of years because the expectancy of life of the judges and of their consorts is about the same, so that that should just about even things up. As to the other provision, how many of the judges will exercise the option, we do not know. It is only those who will have made the option who will have created a situation whereby if they die in office their widows will receive the pension. It is not possible to make any estimate, but it was not looked upon by the treasury officials as being serious.

The minister seems to be under the impression that I was referring
to superior court appointments made by himself when I spoke of defeated candidates. That was farthest from my mind. But there have been quite a number of district court and county court judgeship appointments which singularly enough have gone to men who, at least having other qualifications, have been mixed up in'politics and been defeated in an election. I was not referring in any way to superior court appointments, for I know that in our own province, and I have mentioned this on a previous occasion, the appointments have been most satisfactory.
I would like to place two matters very shortly before the minister in regard to judicial appointments in county court and district court jurisdictions. The first is this, that no appointment should be made of barristers practising in the locality in which they will serve as judges. That is a very important matter. I find that wherever a judge is appointed to preside in a district court or county court in the town or area in which he practised law it takes a very considerable period of time before litigants appearing before him, who at any time had litigation on the other side against that judge while he was practising, are convinced that his judgment has not been influenced thereby. I am not saying that I know of any such case; far be it from me, but as I said, it is very important that people when they seek access to the courts should not only get justice but believe that they get justice.
And that the judgments are handed down in reasonable time.

In that respect there has been .much improvement since the Minister of Justice became interested and let it be known that where there has been a delay of over two or three months in handing down a judgment the judge should endeavour at an early day to bring down his judgment. I have no doubt that the minister has in the past suffered from delayed judgments, and bringing about that reform he has certainly done something that has met with the approval of the bar society. Men are appointed who appear to have qualifications requisite for the bench; they' are believed to have the judicial temperament; but when they get on the bench there are some who occasionally display' a temperament far removed from what can be properly designated as judicial. I suggest that the minister have his law officers give consideration, in so far as the lower judgeships are concerned in any event, to the adoption of a system similar to that followed in Great Britain, where in most cases before a man is appointed to the bench he has had the opportunity of serving in a junior judicial position.
*>260
Judges Act

In Britain they have the recorder system: the Lord Chancellor assigns or appoints an outstanding member of the bar to preside over a series of assizes and courts, and it can then be ascertained whether or not he possesses the judicial temperament. I do not know to what extent that course could be followed in this country, but I believe that if something in the nature of promotions could be provided for it would greatly improve the judiciary; by which I mean, it would give the opportunity to outstanding men in the county and district courts to look forward to the day when they might expect to be given the opportunity to accept appointment to the superior court, and, if accepted, to be appointed. The minister has followed that course in two instances that I know of, one in Alberta, the other in British Columbia, and has elevated to the superior court, district or county court judges. I think it merits expansion, and certainly consideration to that end, for by both the appointments to which I have made reference the superior courts have certainly been enriched.

I would add just a word in support of the views of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I am sorry that the Minister of Finance is not present at this discussion; were he here he might receive some useful suggestions regarding the payments of pensions to the citizens of Canada who must look to him for their payments.
I find that in the civil estimates the federal government appropriates this year a matter of $31 million to look after the 190,000 old people in this country who, after passing the age of seventy, must go through a means test and demonstrate that they have not been able to acquire enough to keep them in the evening of life, and that their dependents are not prepared to care for them, and under those circumstances the federal government votes around two hundred dollars per person to tide them through the evening of life. The Minister of Justice is much more generous than the Minister of Finance. His top ceiling in pensions for judges is a matter of $15,000 per year. It has always been difficult for me to understand why, when one honoured Canadian must have $15,000 a year as a pension, it can be expected that 190,000 must get by on an average of around three hundred dollars. I hope that when the Minister of Justice is in conference with his other colleagues in the government, particularly the Minister of Finance, something will be done to carry out the principles which are now being discussed by some legal members of the house in dealing with old age pensioners who must get their help from the Minister of Finance and from

the provinces. The total from the civil estimates is around thirty-one millions, from the war appropriation, around seven millions, and from the provinces twelve millions, to care for 190,000 of our honoured citizens-which is a very small amount compared with the terms in which we are speaking in dealing with the retiring judges and their ladies.

I do not want to be put in the position of being misunderstood in this matter. We were discussing judges and judges' salaries and the position of the judiciary, and so far as the old age pensions of the country are concerned, I do not think the matter is relevant under this item. But I have never for one single minute indicated any belief that the old age pensions now paid are adequate. I have always felt that they were totally inadequate, and if the opportunity is given me I shall support as strongly as I can any move to raise the pensions to the old people of this country.

This is the grant to the chief constables' association, and I wish at this time to make a plea for consideration being given to the city, municipal and village policemen who are represented generally by this association. This matter has been brought to my attention by an official of the association, and I am very glad to bring it before the committee and the country and to speak on behalf of that great body of self-effacing men, the municipal policemen represented not only by this association but those in the villages and towns, whose fine record of public service we so often, lose sight of.

should be given to grants in aid on the part of the dominion to tihe provinces to enable the carrying into effect of a pension system on behalf of all municipal, town and village policemen for whom there is no pension provision now in effect. Efficiency would be promoted if the system followed in the United Kingdom were carried out in this country. These municipal police forces cooperate with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and with the provincial police force in the provinces in which they are established. That cooperation could be carried to the point where there would be increased efficiency if provision were made similar to that in effect in the United Kingdom, where an inspector of the home office each year conducts an inspection of all the municipal forces within the country, whether under his jurisdiction or not.
If any of the municipal forces are below the standard of efficiency demanded by the home office as reported on by the inspecting officer then that particular municipal police force is denied the pension provisions. I do not expect any final answer from the minister in regard to this matter. In view, however, of the definite increase in juvenile delinquency- true, there was a decrease last year-and the tremendous increase since 1930 of serious crimes, indictable offences and the like in proportion to population, few would object if by a small expenditure a greater control over the efficiency of these forces could be ensured. We could take one of the senior officers in the criminal investigation branch in Ottawa and put him in charge of this work. The result would be that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police would have charge of the prosecution of federal offences, the provincial police would have charge of provincial offences and the municipal police would deal with both subjects and with municipal by-laws; and all would have a common standard of efficiency. Efficiency would be maintained; security would be given to those forces, and it would be of great benefit in raising the standard of criminal investigation and prosecution in this country; in short it would go a long way towards *^curing a degree of equality in the efficient and effective administration of the criminal law by police officers that is not always secured.
I pass this suggestion on to the minister. It has been recommended on more than one occasion by the chief constables association. It is a matter that might very well be brought before the next dominion-provincial conference for report and consideration; for there

is nothing more important than the maintaining of the highest possible efficiency in the police forces of this country.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
There is a matter under the heading of labour administration which I took u,p previously with the minister and

about which I should like to say something further at this time. I first raised this matter in the house on May 1 during the discussion of the minister's section of the war appropriation estimates. This has to do with the pension rights of employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway who were out on strike in 1918 or 1919. Following the discussion we had on this matter on May 1, I wrote to the minister on two occasions, on May 15 and June 16, and on June 20 I received a reply from the minister with which he enclosed a copy of a letter which had been sent to his deputy, Mr. MacNamara, by Mr. C. E. Stockdill, assistant to the vice-president of the Canadian Pacific. In other words, the minister did something following my representations both in the house and by letter; he referred the matter to the vice-president of the C.P.R. and received this one letter from Mr. Stockdill. I am grateful for the fact that the minister recognized that this was a matter in which he should interest himself, but I am not at all satisfied with the reply Mr. Stockdill made to Mr. MacNamara, nor am I satisfied to let the Minister of Labour allow the matter to rest there.
In order to discuss the matter properly I think I should quote to the committee the text of Mr. Stockdill's letter. It was written from Montreal on June 8 and addressed to the deputy minister of labour. Hon. members will note that in this letter Mr. Stockdill endeavours to slap me down for some of the things I said on May 1. I read the letter for two reasons: first, in order that I may point out wherein he has grossly distorted my statements of May 1, and, second, in order that I may reply to his arguments and endeavour to persuade the minister to work further on this matter. The letter follows: Dear Mr. MacNamara,
In the absence of the vice president, I am replying to your letter o,f May 19.
It is unfortunate, to say the least, that Mr. Knowles, who does not lack sources of accurate information, should have put forward, unwittingly perhaps, a version which is not borne out by the facts of the ease.
At page 25-02 of Hansard he repeats four times -in varying form the statement that when the new pension plan was set up in 1937, a change was made which -had the effect of creating a new problem for the men who left our service during the strike of 1919.
In point of fact no change was made by the 1937 revision of the pension rules, which affected in any way the position of the men concerned.
The provision of the pension rules that any one entering the service of the company after having reached the age of forty is ineligible to receive a pension has been in effect since July 5, 1904, and the provision that persons voluntarily

Supply-La hour
leaving the employment of the company when their services are required become ineligible, was incorporated in the original regulations when the pension system was inaugurated on January 1, 1903.
The effect of clause 8 (a) of the existing pension rules, which was quoted in part by Mr. Knowles, was merely to give effect to these two previously existing rules.
Since July 5, 1904, many men have left the company's service for reasons which seemed good to them, and have later re-entered the service, but only those who were under forty at the time of their last entry became eligible for pension.
Mr. Knowles statement at page 2505 of Hansard, with regard to the effect of section 122 of the railway act, also lacks candour. While the pension system was a voluntary one the company acted under this provision of the statute, a provision essential to the establishment of -a pension system of any kind; but when it became necessary to put the system upon a contributory basis the cooperation of the employees was invited and the pension rules were framed by a joint committee composed of four representatives named by the company and four chosen by the general chairmen of the organized employees, and the employees have enjoyed adequate representation on the pension committee ever since.
None of the men concerned had any grievance against the 'company at the time they left their employment, nor, if the statements of their responsible leaders are to be accepted, were they ignorant of the results 'of their action, since it has been repeatedly asserted by these leaders that the men were warned of the consequences, and of the fact that the strike contemplated was in defiance of existing law.
Yours very truly,
C. E. Stockdill, Assistant to the Vice President.
I happen to know Mr. Stockdill personally. I have every regard for him in his private capacity as a very fine gentleman, but I am amazed at the tone and substance of the letter which he saw fit in his capacity as an official of the Canadian Pacific to write to the government on this matter, a letter consisting of distortion along with evasion of the real issue. First of alt he makes the statement that on page 2502 of Hansard I said four times in varying forms that the provision of clause 8 was a new provision inserted in 1937. Anyone who refers to that page of Hansard will find that while it is true I referred four times on that page-and rightly so-to the new pension rules which were established in 1937, at no time did I refer to the clause requiring every employee to be under forty at the time of his last entry into the service as a new provision. What Mr. Stockdill and the other officials of the company know is that in 1936, 1937, 1938 and 1939 that clause, an old one to be sure which was hatched out in 1903 and carried over into the new rules, was the principal bone of contention between the employees and the
company so far as the new pension plan was concerned. It was at that time that the men were most conscious of what that clause would do to many hundreds of them by way of cutting down their pension rights in many cases and1 denying any pension at all to many others.
Mr. Stockdill points out that the pension plan as instituted on January 1, 1937, was the result of the work of the company with a committee appointed by the general chairmen representing the men. That too is true, but it is not the whole story. The men tell me that the committee that represeented the general chairmen agreed to the pension plan before it was referred to the general membership of the various unions. As a matter of fact a booklet setting out the new plan and bearing the date September 15, 1936, was distributed among the employees of the company several months before the plan came into effect, but its terms had been made final. When the general membership discovered what was the effect upon them of this new plan, which carried over into its provisions the rule contained in clause S, they really went to work on it. The matter was discussed in all the unions of the Canadian Pacific System whose members were affected by it, particularly in western Canada, and in due course they sent a strong delegation from the west to Montreal to wait upon their general chairmen. That was in 1937, just after the plan came into effect. They discussed a number of matters, but the major point that they discussed was clause 8, because the decision which the company had handed down to the men at that time was that their absence from work in 1918 or 1919 was to be considered as a break in their service. As a result of the representations made by the membership to their general chairmen in 1937, the general chairmen waited upon the company several times in the years 1937, 1938 and 1939, and I repeat that Mr. Stockdill and the other officials know that this question was the burning issue at that time, and it still remains a burning issue with many hundreds of the employees of the company.
I would refer the minister, in the hope that he will reconsider this matter, to some of the quotations that I placed on the record when I last discussed this matter on May 1, quotations which I do not need to repeat at this time except to point out that they made it clear that Mr. Coleman, who was then vice-president of the company, said to the men that the real stickler so far as the company was concerned was that they could not afford to pay these pensions. The men who waited upon the officials of the company at that time came away convinced, and so reported to their
Supply-Labour

general membership, that if the fortunes of the company were a little better there might be some hope of their getting these pension rights restored.
On what date is Mr. Coleman said to have said that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
That was in 1939. I put the exact date on the record when I spoke on this matter on May 1. I also pointed out at that time, and I think I should repeat it, that in the years prior to 1937 the pension scheme that was in effect in the Canadian Pacific railway system was what was known as a non-contributory system. The company therefore used the argument that the men had no equity in the funds of the company, while on the other hand the men recall that every time there was any discussion or negotiations with respect to wages down across the years from the early part of the century to 1937 the company always pointed out that there was this non-contributory pension plan. In other words, the men were told to remember that what they were receiving was not just the wages that they received in their pay envelopes, but certain pension rights that they would obtain on retirement. And so the men felt that they had an equity which they had built up by their work with the company over a period of years.
When Mr. Coleman says that it would cost the company $1,250,000 to restore those pension rights which the men had in 1919, I suggest he is admitting that the men had that much of an equity in the funds of the company at that time, and that what the company did was, by means of a technicality, to appropriate the funds which really belonged to the men.
That is going a long way.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that that is going a long way, but in my view that is exactly what the situation is.
Related to this whole question is the position which other employers took at the same time. I fear that I must repeat briefly at this point. In addition to the employees of the Canadian Pacific, I would remind the committee that employees of the Canadian National and a certain number of dominion government, provincial government and Winnipeg municipal employees were involved in the strike which took place in 1919. But these other employers, the Canadian National, the dominion government, the provincial government and the municipal government, have all completely disregarded the strike of 1919 as affecting the pension rights of their employees, leaving the Canadian Pacific the only large

employer which still holds participation in the strike as against its employees in the matter of pension rights.
When one recalls as well the land grants and subsidies and tax exemptions which the Canadian Pacific have enjoyed down across the years, and that is true in the city of Winnipeg as well, it seems to me that they are not playing fair with the country, and certainly not playing fair with the men, in continuing to deny to them their pension rights.
Mr. Stockdill in his letter suggests that in one portion of my remarks I lacked candour because of my references to the fact that the government should concern itself in this matter with a view to protecting the interests of the men. The reply that Mr. Stockdill makes to that is that the plan was set up by this joint committee and that the men now have adequate representation on the pension scheme. In other words, the presumption is that the men's interests are fully protected, and there is no need for government intervention. I have already pointed out that the first time the plan was ever brought to the attention of the men they were not satisfied with it because of this clause that was included in it, and immediately they voiced their protest against it. I would also point out so far as adequate representation on the committee is concerned, as suggested by Mr. Stockdill, that the committee consists of seven members, four of them being officials of the company and only three of them representatives of the general chairmen of the unions to which the men belong. Despite the fact that four constitutes a quorum there is never any danger of the general chairmen of the unions constituting a majority of a committee meeting, because when any of the officials of the company are absent from a meeting they have a right to appoint proxies to take their place. Thus the proportion of four officials of the company to three representatives of the men is maintained at all times.

Captain . . . now receives $20 per month pension from t'he United States government, under their social security laws, as he sailed on Canadian Pacific ships which run in American waters, but from his own company and country he receives absolutely nothing.
Because of a three-day break in service in 1918! In connection with these breaks in service in 1918. because a number of them at some of these other points around the west-Kenora,
Edmonton and some other places-were breaks in service in that year rather than in 1919, I will quote in part from a letter from a union in Kenora, Ontario:
There was another strike in 1918 of only a few hours' duration (about sixteen hours), and in this case no one was fired or rehired, so really no legal break in service, and when the grievance was straightened (in our favour) we were just told to carry on and there was to be no discrimination. To our surprise, in 1937-
I am calling this to the attention of Mr. Stockdill, because it was in 1936 and 1937 that this issue came to a head. In his letter he is only evading the issue.
-when the contributory scheme was introduced, four of our union members had application [DOT]papers returned as we were forty or over in 1918. No member of the International Association of Machinists here in Kenora rvent out in 1919.
I could go on with a great many letters from unions and from individuals showing the hardships which have resulted because of this decision. I could also read a letter from one official of a union, as a matter of fact a general chairman, who says that he is very much afraid that one of the reasons for retaining this clause 8 in the pension rules is that it enables the company to continue to hold a club over the men. Perhaps I should read part of this letter because it relates to something which is a burning issue right now:
It so happens that I was personally involved so quite naturally I had more than a passing interest in the question. I was one of a subcommittee set up to handle the matter with officials at Winnipeg, but we got absolutely nowhere. Although the reason given of continuing this injustice is one of inability to pay-
Mark you, this is a statement of one of the general chairmen.
-I am convinced that the board of directors are insistent of retaining the restrictive clause, so that the company will always hold a club over the head of the employees over forty who might be considering going on strike. Certainly [DOT]they would think twice before leaving their jobs, and if we are turned down by the national war labour board on applications for wage increases some such action might be considered.
So that in addition to the injustice of the whole situation and the suffering which many of these men are enduring because of the inclusion of that rule in the pension by-laws as they now stand, it is the feeling on the part of a good many that it is still there as a club to keep these men from exercising their right to strike if a situation becomes intolerable.
Apart from that, however, I plead the case of these cider men. I am not able to get the exact figure as to how many there are row 1	*
in 1937 there were 400 or perhaps 450 older employees of the company who were over

forty when they returned to work in 1918 or 1919, and as a result of that these 400 or 450 .are denied a pension of any kind. Some of them had worked 20 and 25 years before 1919. I have ease after ease here of men with 35 and 40 years of service but no pension because they were forty years or over when they returned in 1919.
In addition to the 400 who lost their pensions outright in 1937, there were 2,100 employees of the company who had some service prior to 1919 varying all the way from one year up to fifteen or twenty years or longer who were still under forty and would therefore qualifj' for a pension, but at a reduced rate, because they would get no credit for the time served with the company prior to 1918 or 1919.
I emphasize, as I said when I spoke on this matter before, that a great deal has happened to the thinking of our people in the years since 1919. I do not feel that the company was justified at that time in deciding that that was a break in service with respect to pension rights; certainly I do not feel they were justified in taking that position in 1937 when t.he new rules were brought in; but now I say they are even less justified in continuing this piece of injustice. The concept of social security has grown tremendously in the minds of our people. The realization that industry owes jsome responsibility to its employees is becoming more widely accepted. This company is *doing particularly well so far as profits are concerned. I gave the figures on May 1. I feel that as a matter of playing fair with the people of this country and playing fair with these employees the whole subject should be brought forcibly to their attention and they should be urged-if something stronger than that cannot be done by the present government-to reconsider this whole position.
I call attention again to the case I read from Kenora. I could cite others, if I were to take the time to read them, where the men claim that they were given verbal assurances that the break in 1918 or 1919 would not be counted against them. I have a letter from one union secretary who says that their union was very young at that time and they accepted the verbal assurances which were given to them as something which could be counted on. After the experience they had then, they would know better and would insist on getting it in writing; but they have not got it in writing .as far as 1919 is concerned, and therefore they realize that they are stuck. Nevertheless in a number of the unions they are of one accord, in their statement that assurances were given quite definitely at that time.
I am taking this matter up now with the .Minister of Labour because I see it as a

matter of labour relations. I might have taken it up under the Department of Transport, but that would imply that the government could use the whip hand in some way through its control over transportation. I prefer that it should be done through the Minister of Labour as a matter of labour relations. This company prides itself on its relations with its employees and wants to be on the best terms possible with them, but this situation rankles with hundreds of these men and is the cause of a great deal of suffering in many homes. Men are laid off at sixty-five and are denied their pension rights. The last time I spoke on the matter I pointed out that some of the men who go to the company after being laid off and appeal for a pension are denied it, and when they ask for something else the company says, "If your health were better we would give you an extension and allow you to work past sixty-five, but although we are sorry to learn that your health is such that you cannot continue working, we regret that we can do nothing for you." As I have indicated by reference to a long list of unions who have written to me on the subject, this is something that rankles in the minds of these men, and I submit that a strenuous effort should be made by the government to persuade the Canadian Pacific to reconsider the whole position.
As to the question of money, the profits are there, and the amount involved is really small compared to what the company is making out of the war at the present time. As regards the actuarial question, I submit that these men had an equity in the funds of the company in 1919 and that can easily be taken care of. I appeal now to the Minister of Labour to continue to use his good offices in this matter. I appreciate the fact that he did something but it was not enough, at least so far as he has reported to me. The indications I have are that he wrote this one letter, or had Mr. MacNamara write it, to the vice-president of the company, and he received a reply which was forwarded to me. That reply is not satisfactory, and the situation, to some of us at any rate, is such that we are not prepared to let the matter rest.
I raise the matter in this way not to hear myself talk about it. As regards the men in my constituency, many of whom work in these shops, I can say that they know where some of us stand in looking after their interests without our having to do a lot of talking about it. Rather, I raise the matter in the earnest hope that something will yet be done. It is action I am looking for. Despite all the failures in the past, and the adamant refusal of the company to reconsider the matter, I

Supply-Labour
believe that if the Minister of Labour were to tackle it with the same concern and the same earnest feeling I have about it, and really go after it, he could persuade the company to reconsider the whole position.

I have not that personal knowledge of the situation that some people who reside in Winnipeg have, people who are able to make personal contacts with the general chairmen of unions, but representations have been made to me by groups of employees from Saskatoon, and from what I am informed I suggest to the minister that the case be given the utmost and the most sympathetic consideration both by the company and by the government'. I realize that this is a matter of labour relations, but I believe that in the interests of good labour relations the administration should intervene and do whatever is possible in the way of a solution, or see whether some solution can be arrived at.
The particular case referred to me is that of employees in the company who in 1918 went out on a sympathetic strike for a few hours. I do not know how long it was, but it was not more than a few hours; certainly it was not as long as a day; and that one act, whether advisable or not, has prejudiced their whole lives. Furthermore, I suggest that in these enlightened days, so far as labour relations are concerned, that single act if committed to-day would not have meted out to it the punishment that has been visited upon these men in being deprived of years of seniority. The punishment would not be nearly so extensive. The fact that this break in continuity was only of very brief duration would suggest, I submit, that the whole matter might be reconsidered, and the administration might point out to the company that there are other cases right across the whole north American continent in which men have gone on sympathetic strikes and afterwards, if I may use the expression, been forgiven for the fact that they made that break in their continuity.
I suggest also that the company itself would be very wise to give the matter the most sympathetic and earnest consideration. I believe that if it took the broadest and the most kindly and humanitarian view in an effort to reach a solution of the problem the company itself in the long run would profit and it would show that it had the interests of the men at heart and was desirous of obtaining the good will of the Canadian people as a whole.

Just a word on this question; I agree that you cannot settle labour relations between a company and

its employees by discussion in this House of Commons. What you can do, and what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is trying to do, is to build up a case for himself in the minds of certain people. I suggest that the heads of the unions, who have more or less intimate relationships with the personnel direction of the Canadian Pacific Railway company-their relations with their employees are exceptionally good-be left to deal with it. The matter can well be left to them, and I have no doubt something may be done. I do not think it can be done here. I do not think it is part of our function to urge the Canadian Pacific Railway company, with the inadequate information which we must of necessity have here to-day, to do something which they have not heretofore done. I suggest that this is a type of case that should not reach the floors of parliament, much as I personally sympathize with one person and others who I know are very much aggrieved. What I have done in such a case is to make personal representation-I am afraid I have not been very successful; and I have to be content with that, as I think all of us should be. I do not think the estimates should be held up by matters of this kind.

I am not going to bother to reply to the insinuations that I had selfish motives in raising this question. If hon. members wish to say insulting things of that kind they may go ahead and do so. I have a vivid personal recollection of what this kind of thing means. My own father was a machinist for a street railway company. He suffered an experience similar to this which resulted in his having to take on a kind of work in his later years for which he was not physically fitted. It cost him his life. labour relations, and I shall be as explicit as possible. My chief quarrel at the moment is with the national war labour board, which has to do with the administration of order in council P.C. 9384. I am disappointed with the machinery therein set dp.
What my hon. friend is saying does not come under this item.
I am speaking about labour administration.

of labour relations comes under the war appropriation estimates.

We can
discuss anything under it.

That board has to do particularly with administration in connection with wage orders. For example, if a dispute occurs between a union and the board, that matter then comes back to the Department of Labour, to the minister and his conciliation officers, so that it may be ironed out. As I started out to say, I am disappointed with the machinery set up. As I see it, in the field of wage control, and the enforcement of decisions by conciliation boards, under the present administration we are practically back where we
