started in 1940. I think no progress has been made. There are so many of these boards today that one is almost boarded in. I am safe in saying that the average member of the House of Commons, who does not make it his business to keep track of all these boards, has very little realization as to just what the machinery is.
Under order in council P.C. 1003 a court of industrial relations is set up-or at least it is supposed1 to be a court. They have delegated much of their authority, by agreement, of *course, to the different provinces. I believe Nova Scotia, British Columbia, Manitoba and Ontario have agreements whereby the provisions of P.C. 1003 are within the control of the provincial boards, and the provincial departments of labour are given authority to administer that particular order. This has to do only with union certification.
That is not so bad, but the board that administers order in council P.-C. 9384, which is the wage order, is the one with which I am quarrelling at the present time. I said a moment ago that we are just about where we were in 1941, and I make that statement because of a specific case in my own province at the present time.
Is that the board presided over by Mr. Justice Archibald?

Yes. I refer to the situation at the Halifax shipyards. In those shipyards we are reaching exactly the same situation we had in Kirkland Lake in 1941. For the past two years the union in those shipyards has endeavoured in every possible way to negotiate a contract carrying with it a maintenance of the membership clause. About two years ago I had the privilege of sitting in and talking the matter over with some of the representatives of the Canadian Congress of Labour who were in Hailfax at that time. I thought the matter was settled, and that it was just a matter of negotiation for a week or two. I was under the impression that the contract would have been signed, the union recognized, and any difficulty in the future wiped out of the way. Within the last week however it has been brought to the attention of the house, both by telegram and through the medium of the press, that the Halifax shipyards are still fighting for that maintenance of membership, and the right to check off for union dues. Three yards are affected, and they are in exactly the same position that they were in two years ago.
Serious repercussions can develop from this situation. The yards at Halifax are important yards, for many reasons. There was a threattMr. Gill is.]
ened strike there this morning-or a strike vote was to be taken.. As was mentioned* by the Minister of Labour at noon to-day, one of his conciliation officers is in there. But what concerns me is that I do not think this conciliation officer is going to be able to do much. If it could have been cured by conciliation, the matter would not be in the position it is in to-day. A conciliation board sat in this matter. That board, appointed by the government, recommended union recognition and the maintenance of the membership clause in the agreement. That matter is in the hands of the Department of Labour, and the department has the recommendation of its own board. The company takes the position that it is not going to grant that concession. Worse than that, only last week Mr. Nelson, the manager of the company, called a public meeting and addressed his employees for the purpose of telling them he had no intention of granting the concession which had already been granted by the conciliation board appointed under the terms of the order in council.
What now concerns me is that we are heading for the post-war period*. If we are correctly informed, it looks as if at any time we might expect a cessation of hostilities so far as the European war is concerned. This will mean that a large percentage of our boys and girls will be returned to Canada. They will have to have jobs. If the employers of Canada are concerned only about themselves after three or four years of war; if they are allowed to flaunt the department's instructions and throw them to one side, then I do not look forward with any optimism to the post-war period. There must be more cooperation shown by those who operate industry.
The shipyards are an important part of the economic set-up of Nova Scotia. There has been trouble in the shipyards right across Canada, from Vancouver to Nova Scotia. Unless we are prepared to enforce the laws we lay down, there is not much use in putting them on the statute book. I do not care who likes that or who does not like it. We have gone along for twenty years in this country pleading on our knees with the employers. I think since the outbreak of the war the federal government have been extremely fair to the employers; they have been patient and long-suffering. A great deal of injury has been done the present government because of the failure on the part of industrialists generally to appreciate what the government has been doing for them.
I hear some of my hon. friends across the way muttering. They ask, "Would the C.C.F. enforce those laws?" Yes, the C.C.F. would

Supply-Labour
pass laws in the interests of the Canadian people and they would enforce them. If the situation were reversed, if the employees in Halifax were taking the position now being taken by the employer, what would happen? We know what would happen. We know what happened in Kirkland Lake when they exercised their rights. Mitchell Hepburn organized his gestapo and sent his hussars in there and used force against the workers of Ontario. The greatest weapon the employer can hold over the head of the employees is the economic weapon.
What happened?

What would you call a man on horseback, with a gun in his hip pocket and a club in his hand? If that is not using force, then I do not know what force is. I have been through a lot of it. I have seen the cavalry, the infantry, the artillerj', the horse-guards and everything else they could put in under similar circumstances.
When?
In Nova Scotia.
When?

On four occasions, in 1922, 1923 and 1925. They barbed-wired that province. It is not a new thing to me. I know it is pressure. It is economic pressure; it is intimidation. That is the club they hold over the worker at all times. We have been told there must be a new heaven and a new earth, that we must win the peace, that our boys and girls must be guaranteed employment. If this is to be the attitude of private enterprise after four years of government, if the authority of the government is not recognized, then I am a little sceptical about the kind of setup we are going to have in the aftermath of the war.
The Halifax shipyards should not be in the position in which they are to-day. Three thousand workers are threatening to walk out from essential jobs because the employer refuses them the right that is granted to others, the maintenance of their organization and the right to the check-off. That is the only issue in dispute. It is not a question of wages, it is a question of maintaining their organization.
I am in hopes that the conciliation officer will be able to come to some understanding with the shipyards in Halifax. A board sat on this question, weighed all the evidence and made a recommendation. If there is not sufficient weight in that recommendation to cause this company to be reasonable and fair with their employees, then I do not see how Mr. Pettigrove is going to fare any differently in a general discussion.
There is general dissatisfaction in Ontario with the functioning of the board. I am not going to go into this at any great length. I have a memorandum in my hand and I have no doubt the minister has received a copy from the United Automobile Workers of America setting out three or four experiences that they had with the board. One point of dissatisfaction is that they consider they are not being fairly treated by the man who is supposed to represent labour on that war labour board. This particular letter gives specific grievances and I have no hesitation in giving it to the minister. It is dated July 12, and one paragraph reads:
As far as the U.A.W. is concerned we are prepared to launch a public campaign in the newspapers on the policy of the government under P.C. 9384 and also the unbearable and the dictatorial attitude of the personnel of the board. When the General Motors boys were turned down they requested an interview with Mr. Bell and were told by Mr. Bell that he had no responsibility to the organized workers of Canada to inform them as to why the board had turned down the request of the union. While these board members may be required to take an oath, nevertheless this oath should not restrain them from giving workers, whom they represent, information as to the reasons for being turned down when such representatives must inform their respective memberships of such reasons. If they are not allowed to do it unofficially, then it should come as an official [DOT] pronouncement by the board as to reasons why refusal to grant certain concessions are made.
I am in accord with that, and I think the minister will be also. A union official is placed at great disadvantage when this occurs. I think it can be said that since the outbreak of the war the organized workers of Canada have done a great job under great difficulties in keeping plants operating when grievances have arisen. The workers prepare their case and state their reasons why they think there should be adjustments. Their officials appear before the board, which considers the case and passes on the evidence. All they get back is a short note to the effect that the case has been dismissed. They are obliged to go back and discuss the matter with their membership and they are placed at a great disadvantage. I think one thing the minister could do is to see to it that when the board makes a decision in the matter of wages on a presentation by any labour organization, the reasons for the decision should be set out.
Is the decision given after a full hearing at which both parties are present?
That is right.

The
minister suggests that they have. I just want to understand the procedure.

I do not want to labour this matter. I merely bring to the minister's attention the fact that I think there could be considerable improvement in the administration of order in council P.C. 9384, and secondly I believe there is a lot of overlapping and a lot of duplication of work between the provincial boards and the national boards. I think there should be a general overhauling of the machinery to find out exactly where we fit in the matter of jurisdiction.
That is another matter on which I could cite case after case that causes friction between the regional and national boards in Ontario. I do not suppose it is so bad in British Columbia; in Nova Scotia our problem in the field of labour relations is pretty well solved, as we have well-defined machinery ; we strike a snag once in a while like this Halifax shipyards dispute. But in Ontario labour is still organizing and it has a terrific job to do. They are at one and the same time carrying on this organizational work and administering the affairs of the unions that are set up. There is a lot of duplication with respect to the boards functioning in Ontario. That is the complaint that I have. I am going to give the minister a copy of this memorandum because it contains specific suggestions to cure some of the disabilities in the administration of order in council P.C. 9384.

I will tp^ to answer some of my hon. friend's questions, although perhaps not consecutively because he has covered a lot of territory in a short time.
There are two national organizations, the war labour board and the national labour relations board. The complaint of my hon. friend was not against the war labour board, presided over by Mr. Justice Archibald, but against the wartime labour relations board,

Supply-Labour
which deals with such questions as union recognition and conditions of employment, which have no bearing on the cost of the article which comes out of the factory.
Is that the O'Connor board?

Yes. It is the same system that they have in the United States, where they have one board to deal with one thing and another board to deal with another.
My hon. friend spoke of the provincial boards. We have in the provinces what we call regional boards. We think that the people of the locality concerned know their own problems better than we can possibly know them in Ottawa. I am a great believer in decentralization. I do not think we can carry on in any other way. Last year, for instance, the national war labour board and regional boards on wage cases, dealt with 43,000 applications, and eighty per cent of the applications were made by the employers. I hold no brief for the employers, of course.
The labour relations legislation is a comparatively new thing. It was brought into being after hearings by the national war labour board. First we drew up a rough draft and invited the provinces to discuss it with us because, under the British North America Act, they have jurisdiction in these matters in peace time, which we all hope to see again, and when that day comes I assume that the provinces will wish again to exercise that jurisdiction. We met with the nine provinces, discussed this rough draft, decided on certain fundamentals, and then drafted another document as a result of our deliberations. That document we sent to all the provinces, to employers' organizations, and to employee organizations. We thought we had done a pretty good job on this document. Later we received suggestions of 170 amendments which were proposed to be made to the document. I think some credit is due to us that eventually we fashioned an instrument that received the endorsation of both employee and employer organizations in this country and the endorsation of all the provinces. I only wish that we could have as much agreement on other questions concerning this dominion as we had on this question concerning labour relations. But as I have said before in this house, when you draft a document, even though it may be agreed upon by all the parties concerned, it is something like composing a symphony. It looks all right on paper, but you do not know what it will sound like when it comes out of the instruments.
By law, employers are compelled to recognize bona fide trade unions. The question raised in the Halifax shipyards dispute does not come under the national war labour board, but under the wartime labour relations board, because it deals with conditions of work and the certification of trade unions. They have had an agreement in the Halifax shipyards since 1941. They had one in 1942, and again in 1943, and they would have had an agreement now except that the employer will not agree to the check-off and to what you might call the closed or union shop.
In the drafting of this legislation respecting labour relations, suggestions were made-the U. A. W. was one party that suggested it-that the reports of boards of conciliation should be binding on both parties, but that was one of the few organizations that agreed to that principle. The Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, the Canadian Congress of Labour and the employers' organizations were opposed to that principle.
The principle of compulsion?

Yes. The opinion has been expressed by the President of the United States that the closed shop should not be permitted in time of war. That is a matter of opinion. My hon. friend might have one view, the hon. member for York-Sunbury another and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre a still different opinion.
The issue at Halifax shipyards is not the closed shop.

It is a check-off and a form of closed shop. I am using that language because it is the language generally understood by trade unionists and other people in this country. That is the only issue in dispute. It it not a question of wages nor of seniority or working conditions. The only question in dispute is the closed shop and the check-off. That is streets apart from the Kirkland Lake situation. I sat as chairman of the commission on the dispute there, and I felt that if we could have used a little more patience we could eventually have got an agreement in Kirkland Lake. There is absolutely no comparison between the conditions arising out of the Kirkland Lake dispute and this particular dispute in the Halifax shipyards.
I think I have covered just about all the points raised.
May I ask the minister a question?

Any question.
Supply-Labour
In regard to the brief presented by the workers in the Halifax shipyards, were there only two points in dispute, or were there other points upon which they had agreed?

They reached agreement on all points except those two, according to my information; there remain just the closed shop and the check-off. As long as men are men and women are women there will always be industrial disputes.
And home disputes too.

But I think this might be truthfully said, that we have advanced the span of a generation in the last three years in the matter of labour relations in this dominion. We have at least established basic national principles as regards the conduct of employers and employees, as regards the right to join a union, for instance. We have probably gone farther than any other country in the united nations. There is only one country in which this principle is in vogue, and that is New Zealand, where by law you have to join a trade union. That is not done in Great Britain or the United States or Canada. Many people would have grave fears for our national life if such a step were taken. However, that is a matter of opinion. I am hopeful that the leadership given by this government will be maintained in this regard when the war is over. Whether we like it or not, the impact of the conclusion of the war is going to make it necessary that employers and employees sit down together and in a rational way work out their difficulties, their industrial disputes, so that this country may be able to maintain its position industrially in competition with other countries-that competition will come, whether we like it or not-and so that the tremendous industrial structure we have erected can be maintained after the conclusion of hostilities.
I think I have covered all the points my hon. friend has raised. If not I am sorry.

There is just one thing I want to say. When the minister insists that a check-off for union dues-or "maintenance of membership" is how they have it written in their contracts-can be interpreted as a closed shop, it is misleading.
I said, a form of closed shop.

The general public get the impression that if the workers in the Halifax shipyards are granted that maintenance of membership clause in their agreement it means that every man who seeks employment in the shipyards will be compelled to join the union. That is not true.
I do not think the minister went that far.
That is what a closed shop implies. The system they are looking for in the Halifax shipyards has been in vogue for at least the last thirty years among the mine workers of Nova Scotia.
That is the check-off?

Yes, and it is at present operating in the steel workers union right across Nova Scotia. In years gone by the mine workers and steel workers foolishly fought it; to-day they would not change back. In the United States, I believe in practically every trades union organization which functions, they have exactly the arrangement which the Halifax ship workers are looking for at the present time. It does not constitute a closed shop. I believe the only closed shop in Canada -and I do not think those concerned would want to get away from it-is Tip Top Tailors' set-up, where before you become an employee of the company you go to the union officials. Their arrangements in that organization are very harmonious. I do not suppose there is a set-up in Canada which works more closely together and where the employees think as much of the employers. But certainly that is not what the workers in the Halifax shipyards are looking for. Under the closed shop, for which the miners of the United States fought for years, though I do not believe they ever reached that objective, I understand it is compulsory to join the union before you are employed. As it exists to-day in the arrangement the Halifax shipyards are looking for, after you are in employment-
After you have been working for thirty days you join.

If you want to. There is no compulsion about it. I know that in Nova Scotia as late as 1937 there were men employed in the mines who were not paying dues to the United Mine Workers. Your union officials will discuss the matter with you from time to time, but there is no compulsion; it is entirely up to yourself. I know from personal experience that is one of the greatest assets that an employer can have in establishing harmonious relations with his employees. There is not any compulsion attached to this particular arrangement which the Halifax shipyards are looking for.

Are there
any miners working in the larger mines of Nova Scotia who are not members of the United Mine Workers? '

Yes Within the last few
months I saw an article in one of the Nova

Supply-Labour
Scotia newspapers indicating that one of the union locals in the Sydney mines area were endeavouring to make their membership in that area one hundred per cent. That would indicate that there are some men who were not paying dues to the union. There would not be many, but there would be some. In most of the collieries they are organized one hundred per cent.

I was going to ask the
hon. member for Cape Breton South a question just before he ended his speech. We can judge things only by what we see and what we know. It may be that they are different in Cape Breton from what they are in Fort William, but I have had some surprises as I study labour and try to find out the calibre of the labour boards which are helping the minister to administer his department. The first surprise I had was that the majority of the men with whom I talked had a union card in their pocket. I remember a time in this house when we wanted the best brains of Canada to run this government, and I think we got them, and some of the best brains of Canada have come from the labour unions, and these men have been helping the minister to manage the department; and while I am biased in favour of labour I think everyone will agree that they have done a mighty fine job. I can remember the Kirkland Lake situation very well, and I did not like it. I had some criticism. Somebody told me that there were six hundred men at Kirkland Lake who had not taken out their citizenship papers. I said, "That may be true, although those people have their rights too. If a man in this great country has not enough 'sand' in him to spend his five dollars to go and take his examination and become a citizen of this country, I think he has got to take some bumps." The minister has had to stand a good deal of criticism because of what happened at Kirkland Lake, but he has weathered the storms splendidly.
I am not concerned about Cape Breton or Kirkland Lake, but I am concerned about Fort William. It appeared as though when a man dismissed at Fort William for union activities was out he would remain out, but that was not so. Why? Because his union members stood behind him and because the member for Fort William stood for fair play. I went to the Minister of Labour and told him, "Unless this is settled there will be a strike, and I shall help to lead it." Then what happened? There was a change in the management of that live concern, the Canada Car and Foundry, better known as the "car works." We saw that the man was placed back in the
car works and there was no strike, thanks to the Minister of Labour and his advisers, and the Minister of Munitions and Supply.
One thing has come out of this great big boiling pot of labour criticism and labour legislation which is a credit to all Canada, and that is the labour code. I do not think the hon. member for Cape Breton South will find much fault with that labour code. Collective bargaining is in force, and with it all you have holidays with pay. This code is accepted by members in all parts of the house, or I believe so at any rate. I know I accept it willingly, and an effort is made to enforce it in many of the provinces, not only in connection with war industry but in every other kind of industry as well.
Some people have wanted to replace the minister with someone else. Whom would they suggest? He is a man who has come up from the ranks of labour. He has stemmed the storm in many labour unions and has come through and he stands now as the champion of labour. I say we ought to say to the Minister of Labour in his present capacity, "Well done, my boy; stick to your job. You are winning out."

May I ask the hon. member
for Cape Breton South a question? When he said that policemen had walked up and down intimidating people, I did not quite catch what he said. What did he mean by the remark he made in that connection?

I am glad the hon. member has brought that up because I forgot to mention it before the minister made his reply. The minister claimed that there was no similarity between the Kirkland Lake dispute and this one. The similarity is that in both cases the employers refused to recognize a mandate from the conciliation board. The board, having sat, made a recommendation and the employers refused to recognize its award.
The Kirkland Lake affair was more fundamental than the recognition of a union.

In answer to the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Little), what I meant was this. At the time the miners of Kirkland Lake went on strike, they were complying with the laws of Canada as laid down by the Department of Labour. They went through all the machinery, took a strike vote, and legally they were permitted to strike. No strike is effective without a picket. That is recognized as part of the game, and while they were peacefully picketing the plants and

Supply-Labour

the mines, the mounted police, the provincial police, and special police that were organized by Hepburn were sent in.
What does the hon. member mean by the special police organized by Hepburn?
There was an organized special police force sent up from Ontario.
I thought the hon. member was referring to what he described some time ago as the gestapo.

It was an organized special police. Now, any time a government in Canada starts organizing a special police force for the purpose of taking away the rights of workers granted them by law, you have something similar to a gestapo.

They were not there to take away the rights of workers but to protect the workers as well as everybody else. They were there to protect the workers and other people as well. That is what they went there for.
The men were peacefully picketing.
And no one ever stopped them.
The hon. member is not referring to the dominion government?

No, the government of Ontario. They interfered with the picketing. Their presence was not necessary and they were a source of intimidation, and I say that action of that kind on the part of any government, in this day and age, constitutes in my opinion all the rudiments	of
totalitarianism.
I saw pickaters and policemen walking together up and down the street. Do you call that intimidation?
I am not quarreling with the policemen as individuals. Policemen must earn their living. I am quarreling however with the purpose for which they were sent there by the government of Ontario.

I have a question arising out of a letter I received the other day from a soldier who was overseas. This man was working in a factory in connection with which there was no union at the time he joined up for overseas service! What he wants to know is this. If during his absence the closed-shop principle has been adopted in this factory, will he be entitled to reinstatement in his position under the mandatory provisions of the statute in that regard respecting the rights of soldiers on their discharge?

He was a non-union man at the time he joined up. This is a matter that is of very considerable interest, and that interest is more than academic. I would ask the minister to elucidate it.

That can be done in a couple of words. No trade union agreement can take precedence over a statute. Whether that man belonged to a union or not he would be entitled to all the rights and privileges which are his under the law, and he can come back to his old job regardless of whether there is a union there or not.
Though there might be a good deal of difficulty in enforcing his rights, that is the law.
We have not had any difficulty up to now.

Item agreed to.
101. Annuities Act, $273,186.
Do the agents who sell annuities work on a commission basis?
The sales are made on a commission basis.
Nearly all of them.

I have had a number of complaints regarding agents who go out to sell annuities, particularly to women. I do not say that they deliberately misrepresent the facts, but they do misrepresent the annuities to the people to whom they sell them, because these people are given to understand that this money is always available. The result is that on several occasions we have written to the department asking whether some payment cannot be made, whether this money cannot be got back, and the reply is no, that when they reach a certain age the money is available. I think that the agents who sell annuities throughout the country should be told very distinctly that they must explain the whole situation more clearly than they do, because if sales are made on a commission basis it is only too clear that the more annuities they sell the more money they will make.
There are other cases that arise. I know of two or three. I took up one in particular with the department but nothing could be done. I know of cases that other members have taken up with the department. I know of a woman who paid in for many years, or she might have paid in a lump sum, but she had not yet reached the year at which she would start to collect her annuity. She developed cancer. Other cases may develop some other

Supply-Labour
disease which would perhaps in the course of a short time carry them away. They need the money. So long as they were healthy they could work and make a living, but here they were with a disease which in the course of two or three years is going to end their lives and they have no means of livelihood. There is no cash surrender value of the annuity. They cannot get it until such time as they start to collect on it or death intervenes. The result is that these people suffer severely. I do feel that our annuities act should be so changed that in special circumstances money is made available to those annuitants who may need it because of illness or something unusual arises.

The whole question of annuities was under review by a committee of this House of Commons not very long ago.
I do not know whether that precludes me from making any remarks with respect to it, but it is not my intention to go into the matter as fully as I should like to. However, I ask the minister if the officials of his department have read the discussion which took place with the auditor general, and is it the intention of the minister to review this discussion and 'bring about a better operation of the act The amount asked for in item 101 is $273,186. This amount is made up substantially of commissions to agents. According to the last auditor general's report, $157,500 were paid to those agents. One agent received $6,358, another S6,032 and another one $5,047. Those were the agents receiving over $5,000. Let me say that I do not object to the government engaging in this type of work. I think they should. But the point that I wish to emphasize is that in my opinion these costs should be included in the cost of the annuity instead of the people of Canada being asked to underwrite them. In addition to that, I submit that the scheme is actuarially unsound, in that from year to year we are called upon to pay out of the consolidated revenue fund a sum which has never fallen below a quarter of a million dollars in the last ten or fifteen years. On one occasion, in 1937-38, it was necessary to transfer from the consolidated revenue fund to the Government Annuities Act a sum totalling almost $9,000,000.
I am not going to discuss the matter any farther, because I felt that the public accounts committee would bring in some sort of recommendation to the minister with respect to the operations of the annuities act in the future. But it is evident to me that we shall not be able to complete our work this session, and in consequence we shall not have an opportunity of bringing in any recommendations. Is this question under review by the depart-

ment at the present time? What amount of money will have to be transferred from the consolidated revenue fund in the year which has just closed in order to keep the fund solvent?

I should like to dispose of the questions asked by the hon. member for Waterloo South while they are fresh in my mind. With reference to the attitude of the agents in the annuities branch, we have had, in the last two years to my knowledge, no letters of any description of the tenor indicated by my hon. friend. With reference to the surrender value of the policy, they can take up at any time the annuity that they have paid in.

The
amount of the annuity.
They can take up the annuity, the actual annuity.

They
cannot get their capital.

They cannot get their capital back; that is quite true.
The hon. member for Camrose raised the question of commissions. The commission* that are possible to agents selling, annuities are one-third1 of those of the average straight line insurance company. The commission is one per cent of the amount with a maximum of $50 on any policy. In the past there have been arguments back and forth on the actuarial basis of this branch of the Department of Labour. It has carried on on a four per cent basis. My hon. friend1 has argued that it should be lower than that. That is a matter of opinion between my hon. friend and those who have probably made a deeper study of this than I. When those annuities were instituted years ago their purpose was to encourage thrift. In those days we had no Old Age Pensions Act and none of the social legislation we have to-day. It is estimated that the approximate amount necessary this year will be $50,000.

I am not objecting to paying the agents their commissions, but I submit that the amount which is paid1 and the expenses in connection with the operation should1 be charged into the cost of the annuity instead! of the people of the dominion being asked to shoulder them. It is past the stage now when it may be looked upon as a substitute for old age pensions. These annuities are being purchased by individuals who can well afford to pay for the cost of them; therefore I submit that the cost should be included in the cost of the annuity from year to year.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The last time I was on my feet the minister and I were crossing swords. This time I wish to speak in support of this phase of the work of his department. With respect to some of the comments that have just been made I wish to say that I feel that this type of legislation is particularly desirable and that it has an important part to play even in the future when we may have other more extensive forms of social security legislation. It is a good idea to encourage people to provide for their old age, and even to encourage them to provide a little more than the social security laws of the land' may make available to them. To that extent it seems to me it is a socially sound principle- whether it is actuarially sound or not-to include an element of subsidy in the making of these annuities.
I would emphasize the fact, in reference to the last statement made by the hon. member who preceded me in this debate, that there is a maximum amount of annuity that any person can purchase under this provision. That maximum is $1,200 a year. In other words, it is not a scheme which makes it possible for the well-to-do people to provide themselves with large annuities in their advanced years, on the basis of a government subsidy.
I consider the scheme a most desirable one, and I have only two comments to make. The first is this: I wish the government would advertise it a little more. The advertising it is putting out is very good, but-
Is the hon. member referring to advertising in a restricted sense?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: My point is that the government is not advertising annuities properly.
Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Of course it does the other kind of advertising, all the time. I have no doubt the minister has seen the little booklet I now hold in my hand, one which is circulated by the annuities branch of his department. The booklet is a most attractive one and, by the way, answers many of the arguments in connection with social ownership of financial institutions. Even so, the number of people in Canada who have heard of Canadian government annuities is very limited. I am wondering why so little publicity is given this desirable scheme. I should hope the government would consider it appropriate to let the people of Canada know a little more about Canadian government annuities, which, as this booklet says, are backed by the whole resources of the dominion.

The other matter to which I would direct the minister's attention has to do with the salaries paid in the annuities branch. As other hon. members have pointed out, it is true that some of those who are selling annuities on commission do not do badly. But employees working in the branch fare quite differently.
We are now discussing vote No. 101, and we find the break-down at page 94 of the estimates. I might point out that earlier this year, because of my interest in this whole subject, I did some browsing around in the estimates, and when doing so I was amazed at the small salaries paid some people who are doing very responsible work. Accordingly, I placed some questions on the order paper, and in reply some interesting information was brought down.
I would remind the committee of just one of those answers, as it appears at pages 1048 and 1049 of Hansard. In that answer I was told that the duties of a certain employee in the branch were as follows:
The making of actuarial calculations, involving the costs of both past and future service and interviewing employers relative to proposed retirement annuity plans for employees: the annual vacations of retirement plans in force; actuarial calculations concerning withdrawals, deaths and retirements under group contracts and the issuing of individual contracts in connection therewith; correspondence on all matters affecting retirement annuity plans, office work and routine in connection with the foregoing.
Those were the duties of one employee in the branch. At the same time I was given his qualifications. They were these:
(1) Graduation from Dalhousie university (B.A.) in mathematics and economics, (2) Passed three examinations of Actuarial Society of America, (3) Passed civil service grade 4 examination for university graduates, (4) First on eligible list, civil service competition for actuarial assistants 1943, (5) Five years' experience in annuities branch.
He ought to be Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
What about the salary of this individual, who has these heavy responsibilities, and who has such high qualifications? He received $1,440 per year, plus a war duty supplement of $120 a year, plus a cost of living bonus of $221.94 a year. I was amazed that a man of his qualifications and having his responsibility would receive such a low income for the kind of work he is doing.
I took the matter up with the minister, not only as it applied to this individual, but with respect to other employees and as a matter of general policy in the department. In correspondence he explained to me the difficulty he has with the civil service commission and the treasury board-these are

Supply-Labour
friends of ours we run into all the time. However, despite the difficulty indicated in the correspondence, in due course he was able to do something. Order in council P.C. 31/2595 was passed under date of April 12, 1944, increasing the war duties supplement of this employee, so that his salary plus his war duties supplement now give him a total of $1,800 a year. We are always grateful for small mercies, and I am glad that the minister recognized the justice of my claim to the effect that this man should have been receiving higher pay. I submit, however, that his salary is still not in keeping with the responsibilities of the work carried on in the annuities branch.
On another occasion, in reply to some questions I placed on the order paper, an interesting return was tabled. This is dated March 21, 1944, and is identified as sessional paper 233. It sets out statistics as to the number of plans issued by the annuities branch in the last number of years. While it does not give the figures in respect of individual contracts taken out with the branch, it does give the number of plans set up by the branch, either for governmental bodies or for private corporations. I think members of the committee and the country generally should know about this service rendered by the annuities branch. Not only will it sell very desirable contracts to individuals, but it sets up these retirement plans, into which employees and employers may contribute, along with the assistance provided by the government, so as to make possible pensions for employees when they reach retirement age.
I was interested in the increase in this phase of the work carried on by the branch. In the fiscal year ending in 1938 the total number of new plans issued was six. In each of the succeeding years the number increased, until the year ending in 1943 we find that forty-seven new plans were issued. I emphasize this increase-from six in 1938 to forty-seven in 1943. The figure I have given is for the year ending March 31,1943, and I find that for the remaining nine months of that year fifty-six plans were issued.
This return to which I have called the attention of the committee also gives the dollar value of these plans, and shows that a real service is being rendered by the branch not only directly to individuals, but to private corporations and employers throughout the country. It is partly because this kind of service is being rendered to corporations that it seems to me most unfair that the work done in connection with these plans should be paid for at the low rates I have indicated. I hope that the minister will give some consideration to the two constructive suggestions I have offered. I am in full support of this work, but I feel that the activities of the annuities
branch should be publicized much more than they are. I feel also that the employees of that branch should be paid in accordance with the work they are doing.

Item agreed to.
102. Combines Investigation Act, $28,380.
Mr. DIEFE'NBAKER: Could the minister give some information as to the work the commissioner is doing under the Combines Investigation Act; what work was done during the past year, and what work is being proceeded with now?

There have been no prosecutions because the wartime prices and trade board regulations provide for any activities in this connection. The commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act is now with the wartime prices and trade board and he is keeping a close watch over the development of combinations in this country, if that is possible under the strict regulations in effect. He is also keeping a close eye upon the possible development of cartels and combines in the post-war period.
As my hon. friend knows, an investigation is being carried on at the present time ,by the United States government into the whole question of combines and cartels. I am given to understand that there is some difference of opinion among the governments of the united nations with respect to the question of international cartels. The situation is being closely watched by my department at the present time. We have a committee at work and investigation is being carried on in the light of possible conditions in the post-war period.
I think this can be said in connection with international cartels. It is my own view that the attitude of the larger powers will be of greater effect with respect to the maintenance of cartels after this war. I say again that the combines investigation branch of the Department of Labour is keeping the question under continuous survey at the present time.

Possibly the minister could give us some information with respect to the post-war policy that the commissioner or the department is carrying on. I know of what is being done in the United States, and I know something of what is being brought forth by the committee investigating the matter of international cartels and monopolies. I think we are entitled to more information than the minister has given us. He has simply made the general statement that every consideration is being given the matter by his department, cooperating with bodies in other united nations with regard to this very important matter.

Supply-Labour
I should like to know the nature of the investigations being carried on with regard to the post-war period by the Department of Labour. Further, I think we should be informed as to the nature of the disagreement among the united nations on the question of international cartels. While I am sure the minister will not be able to go into full detail in that regard), perhaps he would be prepared to inform us what Canada's attitude is, what the attitude of the Department of Labour is with regard to this problem.
The minister has stated that the commissioner is assigned to the wartime prices and trade board and that there is not very much for him to look after because of the wartime controls that are in existence. I am going to ask him a question to which I think he should give a very careful answer. Throughout the country from time to time statements are made on platforms with respect to the large percentages of profit being allowed to various monopolies in the production of war-time goods and in the filling of war-time needs. We frequently hear it said that tremendous profits are being made. I am not one who makes those assertions, but I think information should be forthcoming with regard to this matter. If these allegations are true, the country should know; if they are not, then that fact should be made plain. Possibly the minister could answer this question by stating to what extent control or limitation has been placed upon the rate of profit that is available to or can be made by companies supplying war needs.

The Department of
Labour covers a lot of territory but it does not cover finance and national revenue. My opinion is that the government and the people of Canada-I am speaking of them jointly and collectively-deserve a great deal of credit for the conduct of this war on the industrial and commercial fronts. While I was not in Canada during the last war-I was at the war-I have a vivid recollection of the talk about profiteers.
I think it can be said truthfully that if anyone gets under the barrier of the income tax laws of this country, he is doing pretty good. I can speak personally about this matter. Not that I have attempted to get under that barrier, but I know what the Minister of Finance takes off me, to my own sorrow sometimes. I do not object, but that is what happens. I know it is sometimes felt that if you hammer the daylights out of the big fellow you are not taking any chances politically. It is sometimes thought that the easiest thing to do is to hammer the banks. I do not hold any brief for the banks or for

any other large organization. I am opposed to combines and I think they should be regulated; I am opposed to international cartels and always have been, but at the same time I think there is a great deal of loose talk going on with respect to the profits being made by those engaged in the production of necessary war materials for the successful prosecution of the war. That is my own opinion.
My hon. friend will have to ask the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Revenue about the profits being made, because it is their departments that administer the income tax laws of this country. If he wants information about depreciation being allowed, I believe that would come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Munitions and Supply.
In order to give my own viewpoint as to the direction in which we are moving in connection -with the investigation of combines in this country, I think I had better quote a letter which I wrote to Mr. McGregor, commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act, on May 22 of this year. It reads:
Problems relating to international trade combinations such as international cartels and international patent arrangements have assumed great significance because of the possible effect of such arrangements on employment and domestic and foreign trade. Already international discussions on the expert level have brought forward proposals on which w-e are not as yet in a position to give an informed judgment.
No comprehensive study has been made in Canada of the various aspects of the problems involved and no steps have been taken to assemble information which will be necessary before sound conclusions can be reached. Questions in regard to international trade combinations are continually being raised and no time should be, lost in gathering adequate information as to the character and activities of international trade combinations and in considering possible measures of control.
As there is no legislation in Canada which applies to international cartels as such it is highly desirable that study be given in advance to existing Canadian legislation in regard to trade combinations in their general aspects and to what further measures might be adopted to deal specifically with international trade combinations.	'
Preliminary discussions on the relationship of cartel problems to other post-war economic problems have already taken place with officers of the Department of External Affairs, members of the advisory committee on economic policy and others. Dr. W. C. Clark and Dr. W. A. Mackintosh, chairman and vice-chairman of the advisory committee, have recommended that the necessary inquiries should be made without delay. I think they should be made under the general direction of yourself as commissioner A the combines investigation in consultation with Dr. Mackintosh and Mr. J. J. Deutsch of the Department of External Affairs with such assistance as may be found necessary. In

Supply-Labour
this connection I approve the suggestion that Mr. J. C. McRuer, K.C., of Toronto and Professor V. W. Bladen of the university of Toronto should be retained. I am writing to Mr. St. Laurent to-day to ask if he will make Mr. McRuer's services available. With these arrangements I hope it will be possible to proceed with the work with as little delay as possible.
What is here suggested is a study rather than a public inquiry. Its objective should be to secure basic information on which suitable government policy might later be based and in this respect would be in contrast to specific investigations to secure evidence of alleged offences. At various stages in the course of the inquiry it would be desirable to discuss with members of the economic advisory committee the information obtained and recommendations suggested. In general I suggest that the study might proceed along the following lines.
Study the nature and operations of international trade combinations in relation to Canadian interests and the measures which exist for their control. Such a study would include international patent arrangements. The committee should endeavour to find out to what extent policies followed by such trade combinations have affected employment or the operations of business enterprises in Canada or may affect them in the future. Attention should also be given to the effects of such arrangements on Canadian import and export trade and possible effects in the post-war period.
Study the extent to which activities of such international trade combinations are affected lay existing Canadian legislation and what further measures may be necessary to safeguard the public interest. In this phase of the study consideration should be given to the possibilities of international collaboration in the control of cartels.	.
Study the relationships that may exist between international and domestic trade combinations, and make recommendations of necessary changes in existing legislation affecting combinations of either type.
The letter is signed by myself.

Nothing

As a matter of fact, government policy, which, we shall be told, is based on war-time necessity, is to encourage control by a combination at the moment. The government is not going to investigate even in cases of combination; if I understand the situation aright, the government rather encouraged that there be a combination in connection with prices and that sort of thing.

I do not know whether I should say "encouraged", but I think this might be said, that at the moment we have more or less a planned economy, under which people cannot do what they want to, they act under direction of the government. That applies to employers as well as employees. Those people who talk about a planned economy might reflect that we have almost one now.
I think we have, too-too much so far as I am concerned.

It has happened under pressure of war, and I believe it is inescapable under present day conditions where you have shortages of labour or materials or necessities of life, because it is necessary that they be rationed and apportioned, or prices set. At

least that is the policy at the moment of most of the governments of the united nations. As I said before, the control is much more rigid than it was under a peace-time condition.

I notice that under this particular item there is a decrease of $1,870 as compared with last year. In view of the fact that no report is given I think we are right in coming to the conclusion that nothing is being done about combines investigations. I should like' the minister to enlarge on the procedure which is followed. How does this commission carry on its work? Does it wait for some person to draw to the attention of the commission that the lumber men across Canada, we will say, are getting together, and that these big interests are putting their funds together and forming large combinations, or that the steel boys seem to be combining their organizations? No; but they govern all the prices.

With regard to, say, the various companies in Canada which are producing and selling oil to the public there seems to be some kind of agreement on prices. In the clothing industry there is apparently very little in the way of competition. I think we are moving on from the age of competition into the age of control. A number of cement companies which operate in Canada control through patents the manufacture and sale of cement. Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words with respect to these divorce bills. Without committing myself on this matter, because I am and always will be opposed to any form of divorce, I went to the trouble to read a considerable number of the reports containing the evidence produced in support of these bills. I take this opportunity to protest strongly against the granting of so many divorces on such meagre evidence.
All the evidence is of the same kind. The evidence in most of these cases is prepared by private detective agencies, without the support of any other evidence. I might add that I have persona] knowledge of at least one case in which the evidence was altogether fabricated, and the respondent was paid a considerable sum of money to prevent his contesting the case. I say further that not ten per cent of these petitions would be granted before an ordinary court of justice.
In these days of stress and suffering I am asking myself if a nation can entertain the hope of seeing better days when its fundamental foundation, its institution of matrimony, is being so lightly dealt with. Can a nation build for a better future when its parliament consents to the ratification of such a state of affairs? The Prime Minister told us some time ago that even when the war is over we shall have to meet the forces of evil spread throughout the world. I agree with what he said, and I believe the best support which we can give those forces of evil is, without any doubt, the ease with which divorces are obtained in this country.
We as members of parliament have duties to fulfil. One of those duties, even if it may not please everybody, is to put a stop to what I would call the most dangerous means of harming society at large. At the present time our armed forces are fighting one of the greatest struggles the world has ever seen, so that our country may be freed from the menace of tryanny, and so that we may be assured of better living conditions and lasting peace. My submission is that the best support we can give our fighting men, from inside the country, is to take all the means in our power to prevent the forces of evil from taking a lead in our midst, and also to prepare for our men a clean country in which they can enjoy a decent living, based on Christian principles.
I say, therefore, that we should reject these divorce bills, and send them back to those from whom they came. Let us show the public, in so doing, that it is useless to ask parliament to deal with this kind of legislation.

102. Combines Investigation Act, $28,380.

When we left this item before the dinner recess we were discussing the operation of the Combines Investigation Act. We were discussing with the minister the various merits of a system of so-called free enterprise in which men may organize industry, and carry on their amalgamation and organization to the utmost of their ability and, apparently, to any conclusion they might consider proper under that system.
I am not questioning the ability of men to form amalgamated organizations of business, but I protest against the continuance of the maintenance of a monopoly and the concentration of power for profits in the hands of a few people, as permitted in this and other countries throughout the world. This country is doing fa.r too little in the way of investigating combines. The reports of the Truman committee and other commissions in the United States and other countries show the extent to which so-called free enterprise is allowed to expand and control the lives of people in world-wide combines. The small amount we have under this item, which is even smaller this year, indicates that the government is failing to curtail the forces which in our opinion constitute the basic causes of depression and which go even further than that, constitute one of the causes of war.
When people in a certain type of organization decide to expand, they become powerful. They use cutthroat competition and wipe out the smaller man. Competition gradually disappears and then they enter into agreements with other large firms with regard to prices. The smaller man is cut out; his opportunity to stay in business is taken away, or he is given no chance to get started. These agreements apparently are allowed to exist in this country. As the minister explained before the dinner recess, the way in which this act operates is for five persons to lay evidence before the combines investigation commissioner. The case is heard and then, if the minister sees fit, he may institute an action against the combine.
I do not know the extent to which that has been carried out. In our opinion too many combines have been permitted in this country. Rich and powerful companies have got control of our natural resources. They control most of our oil resources, our steel, our water power, our nickel and our lumber.

In other industries we find that these people have control of food, clothing and the things required to build shelter. They gradually build up monopolies in the national field. Then when they have overcome competition in that field, they go into the international field. There are concerns which are recognized throughout the world as being international combines with tremendous power.
When the control of food, clothing, shelter and the necessities of life within the nation are in the hands of a few people, it inevitably leads to want and insecurity, a lowered standard of living and a lowered standard of health.
We have the highest standard of living in the world.
Look at the health standard records of this country, fifty per cent of our young men unable to pass the physical and mental examination to get into the armed forces.

I am talking about the development of the natural resources of this country so that they may provide a means of decent living for the people. We had a million people on relief between 1930 and 1939.

Young men were roaming up and down the country looking for work. When that happens something is wrong with a country like Canada, one of the richest in the world in natural resources-

It is still better than most countries.

These people who operate international cartels control not only our natural resources but many patents. The people are denied free access to these. The benefits of science are not available to the people, and they cannot possibly get hold of the things they want unless they pay the price to those who hold the monopoly. There are world combines which are recognized in oil, in electrical goods, and in Canada we have our great natural resources of nickel under the control of International Nickel company. These are the forces which in war time build the armaments for the world. When there is competition in world markets, they form cartels. They are the people who inevitably look upon war time as a harvest of profits.
We in this group have a different philosophy of life. We do not believe that profits should be the main objective in life. We believe that the natural resources of the country should be used to improve the welfare of the people, that the profit motive should be supplanted by the service motive. The people of Canada consider that this government has failed in investigating combines within the country and taking action against them. I should like to repeat what the hon. member for Melfort put on the record the other night with regard to farm implement prices. This was the report of a special committee adopted by the legislative assembly of Saskatchewan as recently as 1939. One recommendation reads:
(2) That, as the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act of the dominion appear to have been violated by the major companies in the industry, consideration should be given to instituting proceedings under the said act.
I do not think it should be left to individuals to start these investigations, to lay the complaint. That is the duty of the government. The government should have the welfare of the people at heart. This branch should be busy investigating these things. There is plenty of evidence of what is going on. We should be investigating these combines, both national and international, just as is being done in the United States. If that were done the people would have more confidence in the operations of this department and of the government.

I am convinced that with the desire of the Canadian people to obtain more and more of the ordinary goods which they
