will wish to consume in times of peace we shall be able to find employment for the men who are discharged from the armed services, provided that they are properly trained, and I suggest to the minister and to the administration that the closest possible liaison should be established between the Department of National Defence and the vocational training branch of the Department of Labour so that the training and education of these men will run along smoothly on the cessation of hostilities.

All the things my hon. friend suggests are already being done. Through the agency of the war emergency training programme we have trained 250,000 persons for industry alone; in addition we have trained
41,000	for the army, 65,000 for the air force and 8,000 for the navy. We have carried out the basic training for aircrew and ground forces. At this moment there is an interdepartmental committee of the Department of Pensions and National Health, the Department of Labour and representatives of the armed forces who are continually working on this problem which my hon. friend has mentioned. I think it is correct to say that no other nation is as well prepared as Canada in its training programme for the rehabilitation of the armed forces. I say that with the knowledge of one who has passed through the period of the establishment of the war emergency training' programme and the erection of the largest industrial structure we have had in the history of this country. I have no fears whatsoever as to the ability of the dominion in cooperation with the provinces and the municipalities to provide training for every service man who desires to take it. But my hon. friend has perhaps already heard that out of 150,000 already discharged from the armed forces only 3,000 have so far availed themselves of the training facilities provided by the federal government, which reminds one of what happened after the last war, that many men and women will go back to their former vocations without utilizing the facilities provided by the government of this country. I am glad that my hon. friend has raised this question, because I can assure him and the people of this dominion that we have established a firm foundation for a training policy necessary for the rehabilitation of the men and women discharged from the armed forces.

May I ask the minister what plans he and his department have for taking over the vocational training now being carried on by the army in Saskatoon, for example. You have there a very fine set-up. If peace
^Mr. Bence.]
is declared within six months, what steps will the department take to utilize that set-up which is a going concern in the city of Saskatoon?
As a matter of fact, we are already utilizing it. We have taken it over from the army and are going to continue to use it, I understand, for the training of exservicemen discharged from the forces.

I am glad to hear the minister say that he is interested in training the men of the armed forces for the various trades and arts. May I point out to him a matter that has come to my attention recently? I refer to the necessity of getting training centres such as have been mentioned established in the rural areas. As we all know, the war has drained off our rural population to the cities and towns, with the result that nearly all our country villages and towns and rural areas have been deprived of their manpower to an alarming degree-plumbers, tinsmiths, blacksmiths, electricians, cement workers and many other tradesmen. A survey has been made of my county. Unfortunately I have not the figures here, but the survey showed how many men in the various trades could be employed within an area of ten square miles. The particulars given to me were alarming.
I believe that one of our biggest problems in the post-war period will be to rebuild the country villages and small towns in the rural areas. The life-blood of every nation is furnished by these rural centres and if the rural centres are successful, agriculture, which is our greatest industry, will be successful. But we all realize how our country villages and towns have been dwindling in population during the war and how greatly their economy has been disturbed, as well as the privileges, conveniences and enjoyments of the people who live in our rural centres. The war has taken our young people away from the rural centres into the armed forces and into munitions plants in the larger centres where lines of work are now open to them which will be closed when peace comes. I think we all realize the problem that we must face in getting our young people back into the rural centres in order to take up their life there once more. The success of social life in rural centres depends upon the church, the school, the small community enterprises. I trust that this government will prepare for repopulating our rural areas in the post-war period. There is a much greater requirement for that than probably any other phase of our national life. You cannot get people to live in the rural centres unless you get them interested and keep them busy at work which they enjoy. You must bring to-day, much more

Supply-Labour
than we have for the past twenty-five years, to people in the rural centres the services to which they have been accustomed in the last few years in the larger centres.
We look at some rural area to-day, depleted as it is of young people, where the father or the aged person who carries on agricultural pursuits, the blacksmith and the tradesmen having left his community, finds difficulty in making repairs. If you took a survey of a rural district and found what the farmer particularly needs by way of improvements, it would impress you with the necessity of the tradesman and the artisan. I believe the best way is not to train in the larger centres but to take the trade schools and educational facilities right out to the smaller areas. If, for instance, we went to Kemptville agricultural college, looked at the record of their graduates and found out how large a percentage of them have returned to rural life and become specialists in their own business as compared with the graduates of any of the larger colleges, we would see how alarming the comparison is and how much to the benefit of the rural district their training is. With this country as extensive as it is, with agriculture playing so prominent a part, we should take more to the rural areas by way of trades and businesses, so that we may rebuild the little country centres, so that we may improve the lot of agriculture, because we must depend upon agriculture to provide a fundamental place for our -man-power policy in the future life of Canada, and we should specialize in this work. I would draw the attention of the minister therefore, to the importance not only of building trade schools in the large centres but of locating them in the smaller centres, so that while smaller in size they will be greater in number.

I think the hon. member for Saskatoon City raised a very important point, and we should not too complacently assume that we have solved the problem to which he referred. I understand that with a view to the rehabilitation of the veteran the new Department of Veterans' Affairs has been set up. That department will attend exclusively to the retraining of service personnel. The item under discussion has to do with something which should be carried forward into the post-war period. I fear that our vocational plans are based on the emergency of war and that, as happened after the last war, immediately the service personnel have been taken care of or as their welcome by the public wears out on the basis of being service personnel, the machinery set up will gradually disappear.
The minister in his answer stated that we are to-day in a better position from the point of view of vocational training than ever before in the history of the country. That is true, and in order to improve what we had we did not have to do very much, because when this war broke out, in 1939, there were very few vocational training facilities in any section of Canada, and a good job was done in setting up emergency machinery to train both our service personnel and those who went into war industry. It was, I repeat, a good job done in a hurry. When the war ceases, practically all the
250,000	persons who have been trained for war industry and other pursuits connected therewith will have to be retrained. The jobs they are doing to-day are war-time jobs, and when the war machine stops, when they will no longer be making shells and Bren guns and the other things they specialize in to-day, they will have to be routed back to our peace-time economy to produce some other article, and it is going to require special training. It is not a job which will come within the purview of the Department of Veterans' Affairs. In my opinion the retraining of those in war industry will fall to the lot of the Department of Labour. The danger as I see it is that, when you have two or three departments, whose jurisdiction and duties are not clearly defined, handling the one problem, the tendency will be to pass it from one to the other and as a result no one is going to do very much about it. I believe that the pressure of public opinion will force us to take care of the service personnel, but I am still somewhat sceptical about the retraining of those in war industries, who will be coming back to us in much greater numbers than service personnel. There is a big retraining job to be done there, and I am not too confident of the capacity of the machinery and the equipment which the Department of Labour will have available to do that job.
I have in mind one emergency programme which is set up under the Department of Labour and which I hope will be carried on after the war. I refer to the emergency training programme established in the coal mines of Nova Scotia. That is a war emergency programme. It is done through the duress of war. My assumption and that of most of the people affected is that when the emergency in fuel disappears that training scheme likewise will go by the board. I am in hopes that * under this vote, which should be much larger, not only will the Department of Labour carry on that programme of apprenticeship which
Supply-Labour

was started in the coal mines of Nova Scotia, but that it will be extended and the business of coal mining will be a profession. That is going to come within the purview of this particular department. While you may have exceptionally good training facilities in the central provinces of Canada, and as the hon. member for Saskatoon City pointed out, the facilities in that particular city are fairly good, I know that those in Nova Scotia and, I believe, generally in the maritimes leave much to be desired. There was one school located, I believe, at New Glasgow and financed to some extent by the Clark Ruse aircraft people. When the plant at Dartmouth closed the school closed. There is machinery there which should be utilized after the war and developed into a permanent vocational training centre.
Right now, as the Minister of Pensions and National Health is very well aware, most of the returning service personnel coming back to Nova Scotia, many of whom had a job in the mines previous to enlistment, and were discharged from the service because of disability, cannot resume the job which they did previously, and to-day they are making the rounds of selective service offices. While we have a regulation which permits them to take advantage of the present vocational training facilities, in that, province there is nowhere to send them to train. The minister pointed out that a very small percentage of returning service personnel are taking advantage of the vocational training facilities. That is all too true, and the reason is that the remuneration they receive in order to take that course, in the maritime provinces, where they are obliged to leave their homes, most of them having families, is not sufficient to enable them to maintain their home in one section of the country and live in another section.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Is that correct since the rates were raised recently?

It is correct. While the rates have been substantially increased, I submit that leaving home and virtually maintaining two families has a tendency to make these men try to seek employment which will enable them to live at home. There is a remedy for that situation, and that is the establishment of training centres in the areas in which these people live in order to encourage them. In my opinion sufficient emphasis has not been placed on the importance of vocational training. Anyone who came through the last war * and was demobilized knows the great mistake which the men made at that time in not taking advantage of the vocational training facilities that were provided.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: But the basis is very much wider now than it was after the last war.

That is absolutely true; but even then, bad as it was, anyone coming back would have been much better off had he made the necessary sacrifice for a year in order to retrain himself for some calling so that he might have fitted himself into some occupation in keeping with his physical abilities, instead of doing what most of them did, going into jobs where physically they could not stand up to the work, with the result that in a year or two they broke down and were unfit for anything. They had then no chance of taking the vocational training which was available in the first place. A selling job to the service personnel, to those coming out of war industry, is necessary now, in order to make them thoroughly acquainted with the advantages to be gained as a result of that particular programme.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is being done.

It certainly is not effective. It is not being done to the extent that it should be. I merely rose to support what the hon. member for Saskatoon City says, that we do not want to place the main emphasis all the time, so far as vocational training is concerned, entirely on the emergency machinery that is being set up to take care of service personnel.
There is another group to which attention must be given. I refer to the women's services. Very little mention has been made of them. They are coming back also and many of them have taken training in specialized jobs. What is the programme for the women's services? I suggest that when their duties are over in the organizations in which they are now engaged they have an important contribution to make to Canada. In my opinion Canada requires a good many social service workers in the interests of national health, for instance. National health machinery is now being set up, and the women have an important place to fill, as well, in the cultural development of the country, for example, in the staffing of libraries, which I hope will be established, and in many kindred vocations, for which perhaps many of these girls have trained themselves. An inventory of the women forces should be taken and some vocational training facilities should be provided exclusively for them in order that they may take their proper place in the scheme of things.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
That is being done too.

Supply-Labour
I am glad to hear that. You are not advertising yourselves well enough. You should get someone over there to do a good advertising job for you.
We have not the time; we are too busy administering things.

You are like most of us; you have not the time. However, with regard to this question of vocational training, the point I wish to make is this. There is no use in building up a paper organization and telling the public at large what is going to be done, because we are only kidding ourselves. Those of us who will have the responsibility of representing the various communities in the next parliament must not lead the people to believe that we have solved the problem, that all the machinery necessary in the field of vocational training is there, because if we do that it is going to react on ourselves. You must have schools in the different provinces, and so far as the maritimes are concerned, we do not have them. They are not there and they must be established. I pointed out one particular school in New Glasgow that should be reorganized for the peace-time set-up. All we have there is a technical college in Halifax with its peace-time facilities, and it is certainly not in any condition to do the kind of job that should be done in the post-war period in the field of vocational training.
I should like to put the record straight. My hon. friend said that we did not advertise enough, and he added that there was no vocational training prior to the outbreak of the war.
Not much.

Well, there was the
youth training programme. In the years 1937-39 we trained 150,000 young people.
What were they trained for?
Different vocations. I could give the hon. member a list of them or send them over to him.
I should like to see them.

The hon. gentleman suggested that this vocational training should be carried into the peace-time period. That is already taken care of. We changed the name "war emergency training programme" to "Canadian vocational training programme," and we have already negotiated apprenticeship agreements with seven provinces for ten years. He spoke of machinery and equipment. I do not think there should be any difficulty as far as buildings, machinery and equipment are concerned when the war is over. We have ample supplies that will be available at the
conclusion of hostilities. In fact, the department has already put in its preliminary requirements to the crown assets allocation committee for use in vocational and other training purposes we have in mind.
My hon. friend spoke of the women. Of persons being trained who are discharged from the armed, forces I mentioned 150,000, and
3,000	have been availing themselves of training facilities. One-fifth of these are women and they are being treated exactly the same as the men. We have a special committee that is advising the vocational advisory committee in connection with the retraining of women.
My hon. friend raised the question about rates paid for training. This is .probably the fairest opinion on the situation as it exists at the moment. There are many jobs available at good wages in my hon. friend's own province, for example, both for women and for men at the present time, but what the situation in the future will be I do not know. I do not think any of us knows what it will be. We do not know what the position in Europe will be if Hitler collapses two months from now. The situation is one which, all opinions to the contrary notwithstanding, will baffle the imagination as well as the intelligence of any kind of government there may be in this country. I would say in passing, however, that in my opinion the government that is capable of setting up the organization and giving the direction that can best take advantage of the contribution which this nation has made toward the destruction of the greatest menace that has ever threatened mankind is the present administration.

The government passes so many orders in council that we never see, that it is a good thing occasionally to inquire in the House of Commons and get necessary information. I do not think it is a good policy to wait until we see what is going to happen in Europe. We know we are going to win and hope we shall establish the social objectives for which we are winning the war, and that will require certain machinery. I have in mind approximately 6.000 miners, from district 26, in the armed services-that is the latest figure-most of whom are in France and Italy, and they will be coming back.
They have been serving in front-line battalions. When they come back they will be coming to a part of Nova Scotia at least where there is no employment for them. They are going to require retraining, In order to be retrained they will have to leave that province. In a section like that, a heavy industry section, where you are going to have to reallocate to new, employment most of the personnel,
Supply-Labour

there should be retraining centres convenient to their homes so that they will not have to do like members of parliament, work in Ottawa and maintain a family in another part of the country. That causes dual expense. The rates for vocational training are fair if the men are living at home. There is no doubt about that, but I should like to see something in the way of vocational training schools set up in my part of the country to train these men for some other employment. I do not think it is good enough to ask men in every generation to go to war and offer their lives for their country and then, when they come back to that part of the country which they left, the part which they fought for, they are obliged to migrate to some part of the world in order to get a job after the main job has been done. I think we should be realistic enough to say: "When you come back we shall train you for something close to your home and we may try to find you a job in that part of the country for which you fought." After all, that is the part of the country for which these men are fighting. There are no facilities in that part of the country to retrain anyone. I just leave that thought with the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend this question? Does he know of any part of the world to-day that pays for vocational training $60 for a single man and $80 for a married man, with corresponding family allowance so that a man with six children has $126 while training? Neither in Australia, New Zealand nor any other part of the world are the rates as high as they are in Canada to-day.

I am not quarreling with the rates. I said that the rates were fair. The minister also realizes that in most of the industries when a man is obliged to live away from his family, if he is moved by selective service there is a subsistence allowance to make up for the additional expense. That is the point I have in mind. I think it is a point that is militating against the retraining programme to-day.

Has the minister done
anything toward having vocational training out in the rural areas in the schools, technical schools or vocational training schools? Great improvements along that line could be done in those areas. If that were done a great deal of help would be had in the settling of our war-tom country. Our young people would be encouraged to come back to the rural areas and settle there. I think we made a mistake before the war started in that we

did not look after the small rural areas by improving rural life in those communities. Instead of that we encouraged the settlement of those people in congested areas. Could the minister give us any information along that line?

That is being done, but speaking from memory I do not think it is being done in Ontario. I know in Alberta we have carried on experimental classes in that regard. We have also done quite a lot in connection with the repairing of farm machinery in Saskatchewan. Let me say this to my hon. friend. Our first duty is to see that these people get proper education and training. By the very nature of things that can be best done in the larger centres, because, after all is said and done, you have to get a staff. May I give an analogy? One of the reasons why the universities of this country are to a large degree centred in some of the urban communities is that it would be impossible to decentralize the work of the universities in the smaller communities in the various provinces. But the thought expressed by my hon. friend will be given all the consideration that we can possibly give it. However, I leave that practical question with him. The buildings, the equipment and, above everything else, the training facilities, the teachers, are best obtained in the larger urban centres of the country. That is the reason why our technical facilities for the training of teachers even in the rural communities are situated in Toronto and Hamilton in the province of Ontario.

I think the minister will
realize that within the last twenty-five years even the larger universities in the larger centres have done a lot in the way of university extension, and have become aware of the very thing of which I speak. Perhaps he has not fully appreciated the point I had intended to make here, namely, the training of people in rural areas by taking the schools of training out there. I think that has a decided advantage in keeping them there. If he will look through the record of the little continuation school and the high school in the smaller centres he will be amazed at the large percentage of the people who remain in the community compared with the people taught in the high schools or continuation schools or collegiate institutes of the big centres. I think we in Canada missed an opportunity before the war, and we are still doing so by not looking upon the rural community as the place to educate our people instead of bringing our rural people into the larger centres and expecting them to come back. I gave an illustration of Kemptville agricultural college and compared it with Guelph to show the

Supply-Labour
high percentage of the graduates of the smaller college who remained in the rural areas and compared that with the comparatively low percentage of graduates of the collegiates in the cities and larger towns who returned to the rural areas. I think we made a great mistake.
I should like to impress upon the minister the necessity of taking the services for training out to the smaller centres. Even though it does cost more, the return on the investment will be much greater, and it would do a much better job in rehabilitation if that were done.
So far as grounds and buildings are concerned, this war has caused such an extension of grounds for military needs in our rural areas that they could be used for this purpose. They are scattered pretty well over our rural areas. I spoke of our airfields, training schools and military camps. In my country we have the Connaught rifle ranges, 2,700 acres of land. They were used before the war and for the first two years of this war for two or three months in the year. The grounds, buildings and community life were idle the rest of the time. When these facilities are in a rural area they could be used for this very thing. I think the government should not make the mistake of allowing those properties to become idle for so many months of the year when they are there to be used and rural life could benefit by their use.

My hon. friend spoke of the extension classes of universities. We have been doing that for the last seven years in the prairie provinces, Quebec and the mari-times. What we have had in most of the provinces have been travelling teachers who have gone from community to community teaching the various classes that have been established in connection with training in the rural parts of the dominion.
The minister will agree that there has not been nearly enough of it.
Perhaps not in your province, but in all the others.

I think the technical schools established in Alberta for the purpose of training farm- boys in the use of farm machinery served a very useful purpose. I hope they will be reopened after the war. I hope their facilities will be accorded to soldiers of the first war. Is it a fact it is the intention of the government to start up these classes again as soon as possible?
I would say that in Alberta they have done a remarkably good job in the last seven years, particularly since I have been connected with this department, in connection with vocational training.

With respect to the apprenticeship system now operating in the coal mines of Nova Scotia, is it the intention to carry it forward1 into the post-war period? Where are all those people who were trained prior to the war, and what were they trained for? I know that many efforts were made through the country and at that time in Nova Scotia to lay down some kind of apprenticeship plan either in the steel plants or in the coal mines. They never could get anywhere with it, for the simple reason that those trained at that time, so far as these two industries were concerned, were merely for the purpose of providing cheap labour. On that basis, where industries were unionized, no progress was made with that kind of programme. The apprenticeship plan now operating in the Nova Scotia mines is a good one. It is an excellent plan, and well worked out. To the best of my knowledge it is working with the approval of the men themselves and they are slowly extending it. Is it the intention to carry on with that plan, because the department is not going to get anywhere in the programme it had prior to the war in the two industries I mentioned?

I would say that the
answer would be: If necessary, yes. But as my hon. friend knows, the coal industry has caused the government grave concern. Production has gone down and the cost of production has gone up. As my hon. friend knows, we expect to set up a royal commission in the not very distant future, and I should think one of the terms of reference might be the whole field of training in the coal industry.
I see the weight of my hon. friend's argument. I was a tradesman myself, and I suppose largely because I was apprenticed at one time I have been greatly interested in furthering the apprenticeship aspect of post-war planning. It is a step the dominion has never taken before, and it is my desire that there may be established in this country a great love of trade,and calling. I have always maintained the position that if you can teach a youngster to work with his hands first, you need not worry about his future. It has been my feeling that our education has gone too far in the other direction, toward the white-collar worker.
I was trained in a school in which the first thing a parent thought about was to teach boys and girls to work with their hands. I hope the leadership given by the dominion will bring about the establishment in every province-or possibly I should say the reestablishment-of a pride in crafts and workmanship
Supply-Labour

which existed in the early part of this generation. I sympathize with my hon. friend's point of view.

Item agreed to.
107. Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940; administration, $5,375,150.

In this connection I think we might first of all invite some comment from the minister as to the reason why the cost of administration is over twenty-five per cent of the total cost of unemployment insurance in the dominion.
While I am on my feet I would point out something which no doubt has been drawn to his attention before, namely, that there are many employees in Canada who are considerably irked by the fact that there is no possibility of their ever being able to take advantage of the unemployment insurance measures. In fact, unemployment insurance to them is not unemployment insurance, but is merely an additional tax levied1 for the purpose of ensuring that other people will be supplied with unemployment insurance, in the event of their occupations failing them.
This matter was rather forcibly brought to my attention within recent months, owing to the fact that in Saskatoon we have a large body of municipal employees, most of whom occupy the same building. It so happens that in that city we retail our light and power. We do not produce it; rather we purchase it from the provincial government, and then our municipal employees after purchasing it from the government retail it to the citizens of Saskatoon.
For a long time all the employees in the city were in the same position. That is, they did not come under the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Recently, however, an amendment was introduced in the regulations. I hold in my hand what I believe would be described as a news item, from the unemployment insurance commission, under date of September 1, 1943. It points out, in effect, that whereas employees of public utilities formerly did not come under the provisions of the act, from that day forward they would.
I took this matter up with the chief commissioner, pointing out to him that here were a set of municipal employees, all ostensibly doing the same work in the city of Saskatoon. In other words, they were all working for that city. Some of them happened to be employed, not in the manufacture or distribution, but rather in the retailing of power and light. They have been brought under the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Deductions were made from their salaries
TMr. Mitchell.]
every month in the year; but their fellows, who were also working for the same city and being paid by the same organization, were allowed to keep the whole of their salaries, so far as unemployment insurance deductions were concerned.
The fact is that all these employees are in the same position. They are permanent employees; there is no possibility of their being discharged, unless for cause. There is a provision in the city regulations under which they receive superannuation after reaching a certain age. If they become sick or disabled before that time provision is made for them by the city whereby they shall not be left in want. Therefore there is no possibility under any circumstances of these particular individuals ever being able to take advantage of the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act. There must be many other cases in which a similar state of affairs exist. It is not a case of unemployment insurance, so far as these people are concerned; rather it is purely a matter of another tax.
The suggestion I make to the minister and the administration is that the whole matter should be reviewed, in order that persons who obviously are not those who should come within the purview of the Unemployment Insurance Act be eliminated from the operation of its provisions.

The hon. member spoke about the cost of the administration of unemployment insurance. I do not need to tell him that the work of the unemployment insurance administration has been greatly enlarged since bringing into being the selective service organization. It has for its purpose the direction and placement of people in civilian employment. At this time seven-twelfths of the work of the unemployment insurance machinery are connected with what one could call purely war duty. The remaining five-twelfths are engaged in the normal daily work of the unemployment insurance commission.
The machinery of that commission must.' operate very much like a fire brigade. The mere fact that we have a very high level of employment at the present time is one of the reasons why the administrative costs appear to be somewhat larger than they might otherwise be, under what some people might call normal conditions. It was estimated when the bill was before the house, and before the special committee, that the per capita cost per year for insurable persons would be about $2.50. That figure compares very favourably, on an average, with costs in the United States. In some states the costs are higher. For instance, in Nevada, I believe they run to something like $5 a year, while in New York

Supply-Labour
where the mass is much greater, and the population more highly concentrated, I believe it is about $3, although when I give that figure I speak from memory.
We have good coverage. My hon. friend says that some people feel they should not pay into the unemployment insurance fund, because they will never be out of work. I d^ not think any person should take that position. We have seen fluctuations in the activities of banks, railroads and what are sometimes called sheltered employments, where employees have been thrown out of work. The whole basis of insurance is predicated on staggering the risks. My hon. friend probably has some life insurance and he must die to win. I am sure my hon. friend does not want to die; he would rather lose.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He should take out a Canadian government annuity.

But if he should die, his estate would get the money the same as with ordinary insurance. My hon. friend can see quite clearly that you cannot have insurance dealing with anything unless the risks are staggered. In the face of life insurance some people die sooner than others; in the case of unemployment insurance, unfortunately some people are out of work more than others.
It is an old story. People take the position that because at the moment they are fully employed they should not contribute to the fund. We know what happened from 1930 to 1939, and that is no argument why a person should not be covered by unemployment insur- [DOT] ance. If I had my way, and I am speaking personally, every person in this country who was gainfully employed would come within the four corners of this legislation. I hope to see the day when that will come around. At the moment there are about 2,500,000 people covered by unemployment insurance benefits.
Investigations are being carried on by the advisory committee which was established by law with the intent of increasing the coverage of unemployment insurance so that many callings and avocations which many people think should be covered by this necessary protection will be brought within the orbit of this legislation, I hope in the not too distant future.
Are permanent civil servants of the dominion government covered by unemployment insurance?
No.
Why are they not covered?

My hon. friend knows they are covered by many other things which the average citizen has not available to him. Their holidays I would say are generous in
comparison with those given in industrial undertakings. The allowance made for sickness is generous. It is not as generous as some people think it should be, but it is generous when compared with that granted to people employed in industrial undertakings. Then they have a superannuation scheme which takes care of them in their old age. Then, to go a step farther, we find that civil servants, national, provincial and municipal, do not come under the regulations of the war labour board which regulates wages and other matters.

That is the very point I was making. As a matter of fact the minister is really answering his own statement by the explanation he has given in connection with dominion government employees. I was discussing the case of employees who would not be out of employment.
My hon. friend cannot say that.

The minister cannot say that dominion government employees will not be out of employment. If it is right for one, surely it is right for the other. I pointed out to him the case of certain municipal employees. The minister has referred to sickness insurance, superannuation and all that kind of thing. These employees have all those benefits, and yet they were ordered to pay part of their wages or salaries into the unemployment insurance fund. There is no possibility of their ever being able to take advantage of it.

At one time I worked for the hydro commission in Hamilton. That was a large organization and I never heard the question raised there that is being raised by my hon. friend. Personally I would willingly pay into a fund of this description in order to stagger the risks.
Then everybody should pay.
Absolutely.
But they do not.

You are speaking about civil servants. My hon. friend is a lawyer and he understands as well as I the position of persons in the employ of the crown. That applies to those in the employ of the dominion, in the employ of the United States government and the government of Great Britain or of any country where there is a civil service and a democratic form of government. I am not going to labour the point because he knows it as well as I do.

speechtext: In connection with the matter raised by the hon. member for Saskatoon City I should like to remind the minister that the reason why some employees who feel they are in fairly secure employment complain about paying unemployment insurance is that they observe that certain other classes of people-I am not referring to civil servants-in the higher income brackets-
My hon. friend is not objecting to the insurance principle?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Not at all; I am simply trying to remind the minister of something he knows quite well because I haye heard him say it.
You are treading on dangerous ground.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Oh, no, I know what I am talking about. The reason why people in the positions referred to by the hon. member complain about paying unemployment insurance is that they observe that other people in higher income brackets who are in financial jobs of one kind and another do not have to pay. As a matter of fact, people in the kind of employment referred to by the hon. member for Saskatoon City feel that there is less danger of their becoming unemployed than there is of some of those who are

at present earning good money in speculative types of employment. They feel that when some of those people become unemployed the community as a whole will have to provide for them even though they are making no payments into the unemployment insurance fund.
I am simply suggesting to the minister what he said last year when the act was amended to extend the coverage, namely, that to make it really satisfactory it should be all-inclusive. The minister has indicated that to-night as well. I am suggesting that until the government is prepared to put it on an all-inclusive basis there are bound to be certain groups of employees feeling that they are discriminated against as compared with other groups.
I rose partly to make that observation, partly to call another point to the minister's attention and to ask him whether anything is being done by way of studying it. One of the situations into which many employees run is this. They have been employed for some time and have contributed steadily to the unemployment insurance fund. Then they have to lay off work because of illness. I am not referring to cases of illness that are covered by workmen's compensation but illness that throws a man out of work through no fault of his own. Despite the fact that they have made contributions to the unemployment insurance fund, they find that they cannot draw benefits because their unemployment is due to sickness rather than to there being no jobs for them. A good many cases of this kind have been brought to my attention and I have taken them up a number of times with the departmental officials in Winnipeg, but it is not necessary to continue doing so because the story is the same every time. But even though we try to explain to these employees that they have been paying premiums to cover unemployment due only to there being no jobs for them and not premiums to cover unemployment through sickness, still it is hard for them to understand. That simply underlines the fact that this is no time to stop and pat ourselves on the back concerning the social legislation that has been enacted thus far. This is a time to be moving still further forward. What we need is a social security programme that will cover all the things that assail our people. For the average worker it is just as tough a blow when his income stops because he cannot work through sickness as when it stops because there is no job. I hope that as a result of the experience which the unemployment insurance commission has had thus far they may have been giving some study to the question of extending the benefits under this

Supply-Lab our
act to cover some protection of the income of persons who have to lay off work because of illness. I should like to know whether any study has been given to that phase of the subject.
First things first. My hon. friend was sympathetic with those people who do not want to pay unemployment insurance.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I was stating their case.

You were playing both ends against the middle. I know something of the attitude of industrial organizations in this country toward unemployment insurance, and it is not the attitude that was taken by my hon. friend, who was trying to sympathize in a quiet sort of way with the fellow who does not want to pay into the fund. Perhaps the hon. member for Cape Breton South does not know or share the opinion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
The other question raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was a legitimate one in connection with the rule that when you are ill you do not get paid the benefits. That principle was clearly understood and fully discussed when the unemployment insurance resolution was introduced in the House of Commons. There was no objection taken to that principle when the bill was passed. Health insurance is one thing; unemployment insurance is another. In Great Britain they have a health insurance plan and an unemployment insurance plan. I am not arguing the sentimental point of view at the moment; I am discussing the insurance point of view.
The hon. member for Edmonton East spoke of increasing the coverage under the act. I am all for that. In Great Britain, and I think it is true of Australia and New Zealand but I am not sure of that, domestic servants and farm workers are included, and I see no reason why, after a proper study of their possible inclusion, they might not be brought within the ambit of the unemployment insurance regulations of this country. But sometimes you can move too quickly and rock the edifice you have built up. I think the British way is the best way. There they started off unemployment insurance in 1906 by covering just seven trades, and they were very fortunate, shortly after passing the act, in moving into a most prosperous period for the building trades, which was one of the first group of workers to be brought under the act. Gradually a great fund was built up, and the coverage of their act has been widely extended until to-day about thirteen million people come under their act.
I think our method of approach is the sound one and we should study carefully before we include other groups of employees within the four corners of our legislation. I am all for that method of approach. Some people-I do not think my hon. friend is one of them-would rather go ahead in a hurry and make mistakes. There is always a class of people who say: Go ahead1 and cut the red tape and' let us have action immediately. If you did that you would find that actuarial difficulties would arise and you might end up in the ashcan. We are taking steps by order in council to investigate and make recommendations with respect to increased coverage, and before twelve months are passed we may have brought many more groups of employees within the scope of this essential legislation. I want to say this, and you can use it politically if you wish to, that I have no sympathy whatever with the individual who does not want to assume his proper responsibility in upholding this very necessary legislation that wt have on the statute books to-day.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I shall not argue with the minister's attempt at humour in the first part of his remarks just now except to say that I agree with him in his concluding comments. But the point is that if you are going to say that to some groups in this country you should say it to all, and if the minister really agrees with that, we are not very far apart.
With respect to unemployment due to sickness,, I was appealing to the minister on the very basis on which he has indicated he wishes to proceed, namely, one step at a time. The minister knows that I feel, and we of this group feel, that what we must arrive at is social security legislation that provides complete coverage, and what I was suggesting to the minister at this stage of the game was simply one further step, namely, that employed persons who become unemployed and lose their income because of illness might be covered by the terms of the act. What I am thinking about is protection of the income of the worker so that he will have some income even though he is unemployed through sickness, as well as when he is unemployed because there is no work for him. I suggest to the minister that what I was asking for was right up his own alley. I was asking for the one next step that might be pursued by the unemployment insurance commission, and it was my hope that study might be in progress at the present time on that very point.

Sickness benefits are entirely different from unemployment insurance benefits. One of the underlying conditions

Supply-Labour
of unemployment insurance is that the person must be available for work. In New Zealand and Australia, I believe, sickness benefit is separate also from health insurance. It is a different kind of benefit. And as will be seen, unemployment insurance requires a different form of machinery from that for sickness benefits, which brings in the medical man and so on.

I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that unemployment insurance is merely one part of the social security programme. I believe that ultimately-and I hope it will not take as long as it did in Britain to arrive at that point-we shall have to have an over-all social security plan. This is merely one phase of it. I am reasonably sure that that is coming. If this government does not implement it some other government will. That is the trend of thought in Canada to-day. I understand the department is investigating the whole problem.
Last session I raised with the minister the question of the returning service man who goes into an insurable industry. Under the terms of the act at that time-it may have been changed since-he must have had ninety days employment and have made fifteen weekly contributions to the fund before he is entitled to benefit. We were led to believe when this act was passed that all contributions for those- in the armed services were being made by the government, and most of the boys who came out assumed that they had full protection in so far as the Unemployment Insurance Act was concerned. We ran into the first problem, I think, in Nova Scotia, where many of the men released from the services took employment in a mine which closed before they had made the necessary number of contributions, and when they applied for their unemployment insurance they were faced with that clause in the act which precluded them from benefits. It was quite a shock to them, and I believe that at that time the Minister of Pensions and National Health said it was news to him. When I brought the matter up he said he did not think the act worked in that way. The Minister of Labour said much the same thing; and it was a surprise to me until I went over it again. Both ministers, since both are concerned, promised at that time consideration with a view to having that condition corrected, holding that if we were making a contribution for those in the service we should make it and give them complete coverage when they came out. Has anything been done with respect to changing the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Does my hon. friend mean the clause which requires that a man shall have worked for fifteen weeks before he is entitled to the benefit?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That has not been changed.

Then I think it should be
corrected. It is a piece of gross injustice.

speechtext: What I was inquiring was with respect to these advances. Are they, under these war-time conditions, loans, or are they grants that do not have to be paid back?

I am wondering about that because I have had a lot of correspondence.

You recruit a lot of people in one part of the country to go to the central provinces. An advance is made by national selective service or by the company for transportation purposes. That fare or that advance is recoverable under certain circumstances, is it not?

Wherever we make a grant it is done by the government itself. Sometimes the employer pays it, and as a rule when the employer pays it the advance is made under certain conditions. If a person comes from Vancouver to Toronto and has the money advanced by the employer he wants some guarantee that the employee is going to stay some time with him, and the arrangement generally arrived at is, "If you stay for six months, or nine months, or twelve months, the amount of the advance will not be recoverable." Could the minister give us any figures as to what, if anything, was recovered under this vote? I should like to know the amount advanced and the amount recovered.

I have not the figures in my possession. It is not under this vote; it is under the war emergency programme vote. If my hon. friend wants it and raises the matter on the orders of the day or otherwise I shall be glad to give him the information.

I have had letters about girls who came to Kitchener or Brantford to take employment, and who, because of ill health or for some other reason, could not stay. They wanted to go home, but were without sufficient funds, and their parents were put to considerable expense to pay the return transportation. Also there are cases where hospital bills have accumulated.

No one is more sympathetic than myself to young people, particularly young women who come a long distance, say from Nova Scotia to Kitchener. Under a big organization like selective service or the labour department occasional incidents of this kind are inevitable. I have not all the wise people in the Department of Labour, although I have some of them. I think my hon. friend will find that when complaints are made and when they are justified the settlement or the arrangement which is finally adopted is always in favour of the worker. I do not know of that
case.

The purpose of the vote is twofold. In the first place, one of its objects is to acquaint the Canadian public generally, and businessmen and executives particularly, with the services rendered by the Department of Trade and Commerce and to acquaint Canadian manufacturers and exporters with information in connection with shipping restrictions and quotas, both import and export. The second purpose, in coordination with the commercial intelligence service, is to create good will and to induce importers to study Canada as a potential market when peace has been declared. The regular weekly Canadian newsletter, which contains information respecting various Canadian activities, is distributed among trade commissioners wherever they are located, and in some cases it is translated by them into the language of the area in which they reside. In addition, a digest of reports from trade commissioners, entitled Commercial



Supply-Trade and Commerce
Intelligence News, is distributed weekly throughout the dominion. Certain advertising is also placed in various publications throughout the year, both in Canada and abroad, exclusive of Great Britain. The appeal in this advertising is addressed almost exclusively to executives.
Executives?

Yes. As regards advertising in Canadian newspapers, trade, industrial and financial papers and magazines, there is ample evidence throughout the world that exporting countries are giving serious thought to post-war markets. It is deemed advisable, therefore, that Canadian exporters should be informed during the coming year of opportunities which await them in the post-war period. Hence the need for an additional $15,000 to advertise in Canadian newspapers, trade, industrial and financial papers and magazines. In the pre-war period, 1939-40, this vote amounted to $70,000. As regards advertising abroad, exclusive of Great Britain, the increase in the vote is to provide for advertising in Latin-American countries should it be deemed opportune during the coming year. This fund will also provide for reprinting the Handbook of Canada in the Spanish and Portuguese languages. Of

I
have not the actual number, but there have been a substantial number of prosecutions in connection with light-weight sales.

The estimates for the
Department of Trade and Commerce have been increased by several hundred thousand dollars in the present fiscal year. Why is that? Surely that should not be so.

To a large extent the Department of Trade and Commerce is a peace-time department. But to an extent not realized by many people this department has been actively engaged in various branches of war work. We are asking for a great deal more money this year on account of the expansion we have planned, and are putting into effect, in connection with various branches of the department. In one

item there is an increased expenditure for next year of over $300,000. That is for the enlargement and extension of trade commissioner services. I mention only. that one item, in passing.

Throughout the auditor ' general's report mention is made of considerable amounts of money that are paid to the International Business Machine company of Toronto for the rental of machines. According to the auditor general's report for 1943 the Department of Trade and Commerce paid the International Business Machine company of Toronto $45,562 in one instance and $23,250 in another. I do not know whether my question properly comes under this item, but I notice on page 189 of the estimates details in connection with the cost of baking the census in 1941. Would the minister tell us what steps would have to be taken to recognize Canadian citizenship in the taking of the census? During the discussion of the estimates of the Department of National War Services we had a lengthy debate on an item for the development of cooperation in Canadian citizenship. Under another department, the department of immigration, those entering this country and desiring to be naturalized are dealt with. Then the census is taken under the Department of Trade and Commerce, and in the census only racial origin, not Canadian citizenship, is recognized. I have thought for many years that something should be done by the government to recognize Canadian citizenship. Had we done that in past years we would not have many of the difficulties which we have to-day, and the difficulties leading to disunity in this country might have been avoided- if we had recognized Canadian citizenship. I have pointed out in past discussions in this house that United States citizenship has been recognized in that new and cosmopolitan country to the south of us. Would the minister tell us what steps would have to be taken to recognize Canadian citizenship in Canada, and whether so far any steps have been taken to coordinate the work of the various departments dealing with naturalization, racial origin and citizenship?
Possibly the hon. member is mixing Canadian nationals and racial origin. Through the census we secure the number of Canadian nationals.
What do you mean by Canadian nationals?
The number of people who are legally Canadians by birth or naturalization. In the census, figures are taken as to their racial origin.
Perhaps the minister will explain what constitutes a Canadian citizen in the taking of the census.
There is a special act of parliament which defines what a Canadian national is.

What act is it? I find all across Canada people who do not appreciate our not recognizing Canadian citizenship.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
I am sure that the Secretary of State would give my hon. friend a copy of the act.
Perhaps he could answer the question.

I am not sure that I caught the question. I think it referred to taking the census. Citizenship was described not as qua Canadian but qua country of origin. Of course, when we conferred Canadian citizenship in 1914 we conferred nationality not only in Canada, but throughout the commonwealths of the empire. The old from of naturalization papers had application only to Canada. Since 1914, however, they are recognized and have a nationality which extends to all the commonwealths within the British commonwealth of nations. I am afraid that does not give the clear explanation which has been referred to, why a person is described as, perhaps, a Ruthenian in the census, but I am afraid I cannot give any clearer explanation than that.
What I want to know, first of all, is whether a citizen can be recognized as a Canadian, and, if so, what constitutes, not a British subject, but a Canadian citizen.

If I am correct in my
recollection, there was a statute known as the Canadian Nationals Act, passed approximately in 1922. I should not like to give a definite answer about it. I did not expect to participate in this discussion. I think, however, the Canadian Nationals Act gives a clear definition.

Can the Minister of
Justice clear it up? It is a question which is raised all across Canada to-day. I do not want to hold up the estimates, but I should like to have this point cleared up, because a good many people do not appreciate that Canadian citizenship is recognized as such in this country to-day.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I recently looked at the act which is called the Canadian Nationals Act. I think it is unsatisfactory, and it will be desirable to have something more specific in that connection to determine just, what is a Canadian national, how that qualification is acquired, and what it means.

The point is that the question should be determined before we have another census, and provision made whereby such Canadian citizenship caa be recognized.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I believe you will find that a Canadian national is a British subject who happens to be residing in Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am surprised that there has been so much confusion about this matter since the last census The difficulty may be the failure of the authorities to give sufficient publicity to what was the case so far as that census was concerned. I was not a member of parliament at the time the census was taken; I submitted myself for employment in connection with that work as an enumerator, and I have a vivid recollection of this point Among the many columns on that broad sheet we enumerators went around with were the two specific columns which are under discussion now: the one was headed, "Racial origin," the other was headed. "Nationality." Apparently more attention has been attracted to that column, "Racial origin " in which I, for example, who have thirteen generations of forebears on this side of the water, put down "English"; but in the column, "Nationality," Canadian was definitely the term that was not only accepted and recognized but demanded by the regulations which were supplied to the enumerators who went out on that job. The question as to who qualifies as a Canadian has already been referred to by the Minister of Justice when he said that a Canadian is a British subject who is five years domiciled in Canada. I recall cases of people whose domicile formerly had been England, who had not been in this country for five years, and were put down as English so far as nationality is concerned. A person bom in England who had been here more than five years was put down as a Canadian There was no reference on the census sheet to "British subject"; in the matter of nationality it was English, Canadian, American, or what have you. My contention is that the regulations for the taking of the census on this point are satisfactory. I only hope that the confusion which has existed can be cleared up by more publicity being given to the fact that what the hon. member for Souris is rightly asking for is already the case. There is such a thing as Canadian citizenship, Canadian nationality, but even after that has been established one can hardly get away from the fact that if he goes back far enough he has a racial origin which is something other than Canadian, unless he happens to have the honour of being a full-blooded Indian.

I think there is a great deal in what the hon. member for Souris has said. The question is not clear at all, and those of us who were bom in the old1 country find that out when we cross to the United States; no matter how long you have lived in this country, if you were not born here, when you enter the United States you are looked upon

Supply-Trade and Commerce
as a citizen of the country in which you were born; and I have always been a little incensed in crossing the line, because personally I have been residing in Canada longer than I lived in Scotland. I remember crossing the line three years ago, and when the United States immigration officer said, " What nationality are you?", I straightened out a little and said; " I am a Canadian." He said, " Oh, no; not with a tongue like that." Be that as it may, the fact remains that the Canadian national is not recognized by other countries; the matter has not been made clear, and I am very glad to hear the Minister of Justice say that he will take note of the act and have it brought up to date. I want to associate myself with the views of the hon. member for Souris.

Has	the
department taken any steps to restore the ferry service between Parrsboro, Kingsport and Wolfville. which has been in operation for forty years. It was contributed to by the provincial and the federal governments in equal amounts. A special boat was built and named after these three towns, ports of call. That boat was known as the Kipawo-representing a combination of the names Kingsport, Parrsboro and Wolfville-and1 I understand it was the only service for which subsidy was discontinued in all Canada. There has always been urgent necessity for that service, but that necessity has been greater in the last few years because of the difficulties in operating motor vehicles-rationing of gasoline and the difficulty of getting tires. The distance by motor is about 150 miles and by the water fifteen miles. Military camps, naval stations and air fields are stationed in this territory, and the service is required by them in addition to the usual traffic. When it was discontinued strong representations were made to the minister from the towns affected as well as the government of Nova Scotia, that the subsidy be revoted and the service continued. There was considerable criticism on the part of the people who are interested in Cumberland and the county of Kings and in the Annapolis valley, and there was criticism of the Minister of Finance, -whose constituency was served. Many people in Nova Scotia felt that the minister did not show that interest which the conditions warranted in seeing that this service was continued. I should like to hear from the minister as to whether the department has plans for the restoration of the service and whether he considers that it was a proper decision to make in refusing to renew the vote a few years ago, in view of the protests made by the people of the towns concerned as well as by the government of Nova Scotia, which contributed fifty per cent of the subsidy and made a request of the government that the service be continued. I should like to have a statement from the minister.
I remember very well the circumstances in connection with the cessation of the service. I am told that the vessel .was used largely for

the carrying of automobiles and tourist traffic, but in any event it was taken over by the government for war purposes. Where is it operated now?

On page 191 of the estimates giving the details it is seen that there has been a considerable increase in the number of samplers, some thirty-three, and the figure is $45,000. Will the minister explain that increase in the number of samplers? They have almost doubled.
It is due to the greater movement of grain and many of these samplers are temporary, handling the increased movement.

Why do you say: "greater movement of grain?" From time to time the same number of bushels of grain are being marketed, or comparatively the same number. There may be a difference in some years. Why do you need almost double the staff this year as compared with last year?

lam advised there was a considerably larger movement last year than there was the year before.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

I believe that the two railway companies have asked that cars loaded with grain be loaded to capacity. As a result there is a large number of cars going through the Winnipeg yards out of which the grain samplers are not able to obtain a true sample, and the inspection is made at the head of the lakes. Has the minister the number of cars in which this has taken place, where they were not able to make the inspection at Winnipeg and it had to be made at the head of the lakes; also the number of cars in which a reinspection was called because of the unsatisfactory inspection at Winnipeg and the number of cars in which the grade was changed at the head of the lakes because of the calling for this reinspection?

I am informed that in all cases a sample is taken at Winnipeg; but in many cases the car is of necessity loaded so full that a proper sample cannot always be taken. Each car is again sampled at the head of the lakes and the two samples compared. I am informed that rarely is there very much difference in the samples.
If there are a number of cases where a reinspection has been called for and a change in the grade has been made at the head of the lakes, that information should be available.

In the crop year 1941-42 there was a reinspection made of 585 cars; in the crop year 1942-43 there was a reinspection of 577 cars. In the crop year 1941-42 the grade was raised on ninety-one cars; in the crop year 1942-43 the grade was raised on seventy-seven cars. In the crop year 1941-42 the grade was lowered on two cars, and in the crop year 1942-43 the grade was lowered on one car.
To-day are not all terminals equipped with automatic samplers?
Yes. that is correct.

Has it not been proven that that is a more satisfactory way of getting a correct grade than the probing system? I have been given to understand that the automatic sampler installed in the terminals has proven satisfactory. If that is the case why continue the two systems of taking the samples?

The question the hon>. member has just asked has been anticipated, and I may say that the shipper wishes to have information with respect to grade as soon as possible. That is why a sample is taken at Winnipeg. This enables him better to dispose of his grain and also to

protect himself with regard to grade. Many cars are too full to sample at Winnipeg and must be sampled at the unloading point.

356. Canadian government elevators, including equipment, $364,557.

How many governmentowned elevators are the government operating, and how many have they under lease? Are there any changes in the terms of leases for the following year? Before the minister answers those questions may I say that I notice on page 192 of the estimates under the heading, "Lands, buildings and works," that there is a considerable decrease. Why is there a decrease of some $80,000? While we were on the previous item I made a computation of the employees. I find there are 610 employees in these three branches. That is quite a large number of employees to carry on the business of the Grain Act. They do not operate many grain elevators. Would the minister give us a statement with respect to the number of elevators, the number under lease and the changes, if any, in the leases and why there are so many employees?

It is a little difficult to follow all the questions, but I shall start out and answer the first two questions, in any event. The management and operation of the Canadian government public terminal elevators at Saskatoon, Moose Jaw, Lethbridge, Edmonton, Calgary and Prince Rupert are under the Canadian government. The elevator at Port Arthur, Ontario, has been leased to a private firm, and the renewal of that lease is being considered1 at the present time.
On the same terms?

No. I can give the hon. member some information along that line. The principal variation as between the two leases is in the matter of responsibility for maintenance costs. I am speaking of the lease that is in existence now and the lease that is in process of negotiation and pretty nearly concluded. The current lease provides in clause 1 (b) that the lessee will:
Keep the demised premises, including the said buildings, terminal separators, machinery, erections, fixtures, tools and other equipment and appurtenances in good and substantial repair, working order and condition, and from time to time replace, renew and reinstate any parts thereof which may become broken, lost, or unfit for use, reasonable wear and tear, and damage [DOT]by fire, lightning, tempest, flood, explosion or unforeseen events occurring through the act of God only excepted.

What is the gross rent paid annually?

I had better continue with this. Further, by paragraph 2 (b) the lessor covenants to:
Make and pay for all major repairs and replacements not necessitated through the negligence of the lessee or its employees.
These two clauses are somewhat at variance and left some doubt as to the responsibility of the lessor and lessee to make various repairs and replacements which became necessary from time to time. The proposed lease, paragraph 5 (2), obligates the lessee to:

Schedule A includes all buildings, except temporary annex and feed warehouse, all railway tracks, except the spur track running from No. 1 track past the feed warehouse to, the bag conveyor, dust collectors-not including motors-except those listed under schedule B which are the property of the lessee.
I may say that a very great deal of work has been put on this lease, and we have been considering it for a considerable time. We advertised the warehouse for lease, and received one tender. We have been negotiating with the tenderer for some weeks.
